entries.title: The Army plans to detonate a toxic lead compound near the Illinois-Iowa border: What to know
entries.summary: <p>The U.S. Army <a class="Link" href="https://www.army.mil/article/296990" target="_blank" ><u>is scheduled</u></a> to detonate a stockpile of lead azide, a chemical used for making bombs, on Wednesday at approximately 9 a.m. in Middletown, Iowa, about 80 miles southwest of the Quad Cities.</p><p>The explosion is expected to create a dust plume containing lead. Lead is toxic to humans and animals.</p><p>On Monday afternoon a federal appeals court cleared the way for the detonation. The order by the 8th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/11/23/trump-orders-the-army-not-to-detonate-bomb-making-chemicals-in-iowa-without-court-approval" target="_blank" >was one of two decisions</a> President Donald Trump said he was awaiting after he ordered the Army earlier in the day not to detonate the chemicals without court approval, according to the Associated Press.</p><p>Trump had weighed in on social media, saying he would defer to the courts on whether the administration should move ahead. He also said in a statement that his decision was subject to agreement by Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand. Though if Sand and the court don't agree, Trump said, the administration would not proceed with the detonation. He said he would hold Sand responsible. </p><p>“We think there has been significant negligence that has come to light, and it is very frustrating,” said Michael Schmidt, general counsel for the Iowa Environmental Council, one of the groups that filed a lawsuit to stop the detonation.</p><p>“But at this point, there are many more resources for people who are concerned and…I think people are in a much better place to be able to get help when they need it and have a better understanding of who needs help than we did before we filed the lawsuit,” he said.</p><p>He said he did not expect any new litigation in the coming hours.</p><p>The Army<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/11/24/lead-azide-detonation-bomb-chemical-stockpile-army-iowa-courts-trump" target="_blank" > moved </a>the planned explosion from Friday to Monday before pushing it to Wednesday after politicians from Iowa and Illinois asked for a delay and environmental groups filed a lawsuit to pause the detonation. Wednesday was chosen for optimal weather conditions, the Army said.</p><p>Here’s what else you need to know.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-990000" name="html-embed-module-990000"></a><div style="min-height:355px" id="datawrapper-vis-oMfQV"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/oMfQV/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-oMfQV"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/oMfQV/full.png" alt="Locator map" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Why is the army detonating old munitions?</b></h3><p>There’s a risk that these stored materials will detonate on their own, and moving them could also trigger an explosion, according to the Defense Department. The issue was discovered earlier this year and plans to blow them up have been ongoing for months.</p><h3><b>When is this detonation going to happen?</b></h3><p>The detonation is expected to take place at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa Wednesday about 9 a.m., the Army said. The plant is around 80 miles southwest of the Quad Cities and only about 10 miles west of rural Illinois communities just across the Mississippi River.</p><p>The Army delayed the planned explosion after politicians raised concerns about safety. Both the outgoing Republican governor of Iowa and the newly elected Democratic governor called for a delay. They were joined by other politicians in both states. The environmental organization Earthjustice also sued to try to pause the detonation.</p><h3><b>Has the Army blown up lead azide before? </b></h3><p>While the Army has destroyed weapons and materials in the past, it has never blown up such a large amount of this particular chemical, according to a spokesperson.</p><p>“We detonate all the time, but we have not detonated lead azide at this quantity,” said Lori McFate, public affairs specialist with the Army Sustainment Command in Bettendorf, Iowa.</p><p>McFate said the explosion will take place after months of planning. The procedure has received a green light from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency regional office in Kansas City. That’s a different jurisdiction than the regional EPA office in Chicago, which oversees environmental protection in Illinois.</p><h3><b>What is lead azide?</b></h3><p>Lead azide is a compound of lead and nitrogen, used to make bombs. About 5 tons of it will be blown up.</p><p>“The lead azide has aged. It's become unstable to the point where moving it or even allowing it to sit on the odd chance that it receives some sort of shock or friction could lead to a spontaneous explosion,” said Greg Domski, associate provost and professor of chemistry and biochemistry at Augustana College in Rock Island.</p><h3><b>Will the lead plume reach Chicago?</b></h3><p>The lead dust is not expected to blow as far northeast as Chicago. </p><p>Illinois <a class="Link" href="https://epa.illinois.gov/iowa-plant-updates.html" target="_blank" >has created a webpage</a> where residents can find the latest information on the situation. Current meteorological data for Wednesday on the site indicates Illinois is not expected to be affected by the detonation plume. The Illinois EPA and the Illinois Emergency Management Agency and Office of Homeland Security will continue monitoring conditions as forecasts and operational plans evolve.</p><p>Brian Pierce, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service Quad Cities forecast office said if the detonation takes place Wednesday, winds would blow the smoke into Iowa and potentially northeast Missouri.</p><p>“It would be blowing it to the southwest across the far southeast parts of Iowa,” Pierce said. “There’s a question of how high the plume would get, which we won’t know until it actually happens.”</p><h3><b>What do we know about the health effects for people?</b></h3><p>The EPA says there is no safe level of lead exposure. It is a neurotoxin that damages the central nervous system. It’s particularly harmful to children, as their brains and nervous systems aren’t fully developed. Exposure to lead is associated with cognitive delays, heart problems and reproductive issues.</p><p>“Lead is an element, and doesn't break down,” said Robert Hirschfeld, director of water policy at the Prairie River Network, a Champaign-based environmental advocacy group. “Those health risks persist as long as the lead does.”</p><p>U.S. Sen Dick Durbin wants the Trump administration to send a public health emergency team to assess the risk and damage from the explosion.</p><p>As part of the controlled detonation, federal officials are installing air monitors and will conduct further environmental sampling of the blast area.</p><h3><b>Will this affect crops or animals?</b></h3><p>For locations that are likely to be affected, the agricultural impacts of the lead dust are still unknown, Hirschfeld said. </p><p>“We’re past harvest now, and so all of that lead is going to land on bare soil and that lead will stay there and contaminate that soil,” he said.</p><p>He said lead contamination could go beyond the potentially impacted farmland and crops, and trickle down to animals, whether livestock or wildlife, that graze on the land.</p><h3><b>What safety precautions do people exposed to the plume need to take?</b></h3><p>The Illinois Department of Public Health <a class="Link" href="https://dph.illinois.gov/resource-center/news/2026/november/18-release-2.html" target="_blank" >recommends</a> the following safety tips:</p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-4b1b1f80-e463-11f1-83d0-11b933b990fd"><li>Stay indoors and keep windows closed for 24 to 48 hours after the detonation.</li><li>If you have a heating, ventilation and air conditioning system that actively draws in outside air, like a school or commercial building, then you may want to temporarily close the intake and switch to recirculate.</li><li>Use a portable air cleaner to supplement your furnace filter.</li><li>Once the U.S. Army determines the airborne exposure period has ended, wet-clean potentially affected surfaces, including playground equipment, toys and windowsills, using soap and water. Avoid sweeping that may redistribute dust.</li><li>If you need to drive through an area impacted by dust, set your car’s AC/heater to recirculate. Afterward, you can take your car to the car wash and replace the cabin filter, if needed. A high efficiency cabin filter will capture fine particulate matter.</li><li>Wash your hands before eating and drinking and take your shoes off at the entrance when you enter your home. </li><li>Visit your doctor if you have health concerns.</li></ul><p><i>Contributing: Isabela Nieto, Misha Manjuran Oberoi</i></p><h3></h3>

entries.title: Parents call for justice after faith-driven Detroit mother of 2 fatally shot in West Town
entries.summary: <p>La'Shon Jones had two major influences in her life — her faith and her family. </p><p>Now, Jones' family are leaning on the faith that kept them close-knit as they navigate a new reality.</p><p>Jones, visiting from Detroit for the weekend to celebrate her boyfriend's birthday, was one of two people killed <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/11/21/2-killed-in-west-town-shooting" target="_blank" >in a shooting</a> early Saturday in West Town. </p><p>La'Shon Jones, 33, and the man. 29, were standing with a group in the 1000 block of North Milwaukee Avenue around 2 a.m. Saturday when an argument began with an unknown person, who then pulled out a gun and opened fire, Chicago police said, hitting both Jones and the man. Both were taken to Stroger Hospital, where they were pronounced dead, police said.</p><p>An autopsy ruled they died due to multiple gunshot wounds, according to the Cook County medical examiner's office.</p><p>"She was a ball of love," said Damon Jones, La'Shon's father. "She always just wanted the best for not only herself but everyone she was connected to. She brought the best out of us." </p><p>La'Shon Jones' parents are calling for the shooter to come forward as they continue searching for answers. </p><p>"I hope that person has a heart. Turn yourself in, or if someone knows of that person, turn them in," Marqueda Jones, 57, said. "It's sad that person's darkness had to meet up with my daughter's light. But her light will always shine, and it'll shine brighter once the arrest is made."</p><p>Damon Jones said his daughter "was stolen" from her family and community, and "justice has to prevail."</p><p>"They took an innocent life, took a beautiful mother, took a beautiful child, took a beautiful person from this earth for no reason at all," Damon Jones, 54, said. "It's important that the world [and] community see that justice will not go unserved."</p><p>Damon Jones was also praying for the shooter. </p><p>"I don't know who it was, but I pray for them. I pray that God touches their heart, that God changes them, that God turns them from whatever direction they were going and walking in so my daughter's life is not in vain," Damon Jones said. "The love and the positivity that she shared with this world still lives on, and I hope that part of her will be used by God to affect the people that did this."</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.gofundme.com/f/honoring-lashon-jones-and-her-beautiful-children?attribution_id=sl:4d45c9fe-1994-448e-80f2-069bb7dee12a&lang=en_US&ts=1795564179&utm_campaign=fp_sharesheet&utm_content=amp30-treatment-3&utm_medium=customer&utm_source=facebook" target="_blank" >A GoFundMe launched</a> to assist secure funding for Jones' burial and support her children had raised more than 18,000 as of Tuesday night. </p><p>A fundraiser launched to support Jones’ burial and support her children has raised over $18,000 as of Tuesday night.”</p><p>La'Shon Jones was the youngest of three children and had two children, a 10-year-old son and 9-year-old daughter. </p><p>Damon Jones said his grandson, who turns 11 soon, told him, "I'm just sad mommy won't be here for my birthday."</p><p>His daughter and her children "were inseparable," Damon Jones said. "She showed up and was part of everything in their life, from school to cheer practice, to football practice, to basketball practice, to gymnastics. The list goes on." </p><p>The Jones family grew up bound by their faith and often went fishing or swimming together to enjoy the "simple" things in life. Damon Jones recounted how his daughter beamed with pride after her son caught his first fish. </p><p>"That's something that truly resonates in my heart because she was so proud of her children," Damon Jones said. "She wanted them to experience and be great at everything that they did, and she poured so much into them."</p><p>She taught her son to open doors for any woman he sees and explained to her children the role of faith and the responsibility of "choosing to be a good person and sharing love."</p><p>"It's going to be real hard for them not having her around," Damon Jones said. "They just want their mama back, and that's heartbreaking."</p><p>"But I let them know that she's always in their heart," he added. "She's always a voice away ... telling you to be strong, telling you to show love, telling you to do the right thing, and telling you that God will bring us through it."</p>

entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams looks to get back to Goldilocks Zone in potential shoot-out with Lions
entries.summary: <p>Coming off the best three-game stretch of his career, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback Caleb Williams slipped into a rut. The way he played the last two games — wins over opponents with a combined 6-14 record — won’t be good enough to beat a good team, and the Lions will prove it Thursday if he doesn’t rediscover what worked.</p><p>Williams was brilliant in those three games and looked like the quarterback the Bears imagined he could become when they paired him with coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/20/bears-coach-ben-johnsons-straight-talk-changes-the-conversation-at-halas-hall" >Ben Johnson</a>. He was perceptive, quick and almost unstoppable as he ran Johnson’s offense to near-perfection.</p><p>He seemed to get ahead of himself, though, after a hot start against the Buccaneers two games ago and became too carefree as he threw four interceptions. Then, coming out of the bye week, he appeared to overcorrect as he looked tentative at times and held the ball more than usual.</p><p>Williams needs a reset. The key to getting back to how he looked when he vaulted himself into the MVP race is getting out of his own head.</p><p>That’s not necessarily how he would phrase it, but he did think he was off against the Saints when it came to pouncing on easy openings their defense offered him and overall decisiveness.</p><p>“I was just getting through the reads maybe too fast, or maybe a little too slow, and you're missing opportunities,” he said after a walk-through Tuesday. “Just pulling the trigger, being decisive — that's something I always harp on.</p><p>“I’ve got to be decisive, deliver a good ball — all the things that I was doing [in that three-game stretch].”</p><p>Johnson wasn’t worried by Williams’ game against the Saints. He acknowledged that he was “up and down,” but arrived at “solid” for an overall appraisal.</p><p>He and offensive coordinator Press Taylor both labeled Williams’ interception as a great play by defensive end Carl Granderson, who jumped at the line of scrimmage to tip the pass and send it floating for an easy catch by linebacker Danny Stutsman, rather than a bad choice by Williams. He was throwing to Luther Burden, who was wide open for a first down, and operating the play exactly as designed.</p><p>Johnson also pushed back Tuesday on a question about whether Williams was hesitant.</p><p>Williams finished 15-for-23 passing (65.2%) for 181 yards with two touchdown passes and an interception for a 100.1 passer rating. There were years when the Bears were desperate for a quarterback to play that well, but standards have changed.</p><p>He wasn’t bad by any means, but it’s hard to imagine the Bears beating teams like the Lions — the Jaguars and Bills are coming up, too — with so little production in the passing attack. Being efficient and avoiding turnovers are virtuous, but that’s not enough. The Bears need Williams to be a dynamic difference maker.</p><p>“When the shots are there, take them and we’ve got to hit them,” he said, referring specifically to a miss on a deep throw Sunday to rookie wide receiver Zavion Thomas in which the two weren’t on the same wavelength. “You’ve got to hit those because it starts racking up throughout the game. When you hit those super explosives, your [production] goes up.”</p><p>The effect of hitting or missing those plays will be very obvious against the Lions. The issue isn’t so much Williams beating their defense, but keeping up with their offense.</p><p>The Lions’ run over the last five seasons has been powered by quarterback Jared Goff and a host of elite offensive weapons — developments shaped by Johnson when he was on staff before taking this job. Defense has been their weak spot throughout, and this season is no different.</p><p>The Lions are 15th in total defense, the best they’ve been during this era, but that likely will slide after losing Aidan Hutchinson, one of the NFL’s top defensive ends, to a season-ending knee injury. They’re shaky against the pass and were managing that deficiency with a fierce pass rush, which is harder to do without Hutchinson.</p><p>The offense, though, is decidedly ahead of the Bears, and that’s why this is going to be a track meet. Williams must outpunch a Lions’ offense averaging 28.8 points per game, and that group totaled 67 points and 880 total yards the last two weeks against the Patriots and Bucs.</p><p>“I've gone into every game of my career thinking that it's going to take us putting up 40 points,” he said. “My mindset is always that each drive, each play, can be a touchdown. It can be momentum-changing for us. It can be the game-sealing touchdown. Let's go out there and treat it that way."</p><p>Williams has tended to rise to the moment, and this is a huge one as the teams, both 8-2, wrestle to control the NFC North. He’s 0-4 against the Lions, and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/04/bears-qb-caleb-williams-is-once-again-the-talk-of-the-nfl-but-hes-controlling-the-conversation-now" target="_blank" >as someone constantly seeking sources of motivation</a>, it’s certainly in his mind that Johnson is still looking for his first win against his former team.</p><p>The best way to deliver for his coach is to run the offense as intended.</p><p>At this point in their time together, Williams is fully fluent in Johnson’s play designs and calls and needs to get back to maximizing them with sharp decision makings, accurate passes and the right balance of patience and assertiveness.</p><p>Not too long ago, he did that beautifully. The Bears badly need to see it again.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Cubs spend big, dropping $240 million on early Black Friday haul to add Trevor Rogers, Teruaki Sato
entries.summary: <p>A Black Friday shopping spree came early for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>.</p><p>Jed Hoyer’s front office spent big, smashing a favorite narrative of frustrated fans by bringing in two of baseball’s top offseason prizes.</p><p>The haul? <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/11/24/cubs-trevor-rogers-mlb-offseason-free-agents-rumors-pitching-starting-rotation-2027" >Lefty starting pitcher Trevor Rogers</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/11/24/cubs-teruaki-sato-mlb-offseason-free-agents-rumors-outfield-third-base-jed-hoyer-contract-salary" >left-handed hitting Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato</a>, each costing a reported $120 million, Rogers’ deal for five years and Sato’s for six.</p><p>It was a statement by Hoyer & Co. ahead of what’s expected to be a lengthy lockout that’ll put the entire sport on pause. And given the length of the pacts, even if the 2027 season is significantly impacted by the work stoppage, the acquisitions are as much about the Cubs’ future as their present.</p><p>The Cubs are far from done, needing to continue remaking their pitching staff and plug a couple more holes in their lineup.</p><p>But two of the top free agents on the market this winter are coming to the North Side, not a bad follow-up to Hoyer’s signing of Alex Bregman an offseason ago, when he brought in the two-time World Series champion on a $175 million deal.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">It’s not baseball weather, as is apparent from all these leaves on the ground, but the Cubs are making news anyway. Here’s a couple two tree things on a big day for the North Siders. <a href="https://x.com/Suntimes?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@Suntimes</a> <a href="https://x.com/suntimes_sports?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@suntimes_sports</a> <a href="https://t.co/HIRGGMImkE">pic.twitter.com/HIRGGMImkE</a></p>— Vinnie Duber (@VinnieDuber) <a href="https://x.com/VinnieDuber/status/2125341496425529709?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 24, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Bregman’s track record was longer than either of these guys, sure, but Rogers and Sato are coming off electric seasons, generating hope the Cubs will better compete with the world-champion Brewers in the NL Central.</p><p>Rogers is a former first-round pick and Rookie of the Year runner-up. After returning from the minors in 2025, he was terrific in 18 starts for the Orioles, posting a 1.81 ERA, before turning in a big contract year this past season, particularly good from June on, with a 2.93 ERA over his final 20 outings.</p><p>He’ll shoot right to the top of a work-in-progress Cubs starting staff. All five guys who finished the 2026 campaign in the rotation are free agents, and in-house candidates to fill those vacancies — Justin Steele, Ben Brown and Cade Horton — are coming off significant injuries.</p><p>Rogers provides some immediate stability, but Hoyer has plenty more to do as he tries to elevate the pitching. Rogers is no Jacob Misiorowski, the Brewers’ ace and unanimous Cy Young winner, but the Cubs hope he can beef up a staff that came nowhere close to matching their rivals.</p><p>Sato, meanwhile, is something of a surprise position-player addition in an offseason forecasted to focus on pitching. He arrives from Japan’s Central League as a two-time MVP and the reigning Triple Crown winner, having hit .306 with a .383 on-base percentage to go along with 39 homers and 106 RBIs in 2026.</p><p>Sato mostly played third base with the Hanshin Tigers but played a little outfield and is expected to slot into one of the vacant corner-outfield spots on the Cubs’ roster.</p><p>Another Japanese import, Sato will likely be compared to Seiya Suzuki, if only because he could effectively take his countryman’s place in the Cubs’ lineup. Suzuki was strong in five seasons on the North Side after arriving from Japan, and his possible departure blasts a sizable hole in a lineup that was baseball’s highest scoring last season.</p><p>Sato ought to help with that and could be a middle-of-the-order bat, something that was perhaps not expected to arrive as the team sought pitching upgrades and discussed Matt Shaw and Pedro Ramirez as in-house options in the outfield.</p><p>There are concerns about Sato’s potential to rack up big strikeout numbers, though Munetaka Murakami flourished after similar concerns followed him to the White Sox, finding success in the U.S.</p><p>The Cubs have had luck there, not only with Suzuki but also on the pitching side with Shota Imanaga, perhaps giving reason to think they can get a productive version of Sato.</p><p>Big spending doesn’t automatically equal success. Just ask Skubal’s new employers with the Mets.</p><p>But fans begging the Cubs to act more like a big-market club can consider their wishes fulfilled after this $240 million Black Friday blowout.</p>

entries.title: Former Lions owner Martha Firestone Ford dies at 101, team likely to honor her before facing Bears
entries.summary: <p>Former Lions owner Martha Firestone Ford has died at 101, the team announced Tuesday.</p><p>She was the wife of owner William Clay Ford, who owned the team from 1964 until his death in 2014. Ford took over then and had control of the franchise before stepping aside for her daughter, Sheila Ford Hamp in 2020. She held the title of Owner/Chair Emeritus.</p><p>The Lions host <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a> on Thanksgiving and likely will honor her before the game, though the team hadn't revealed any plans as of Tuesday night. In a statement, it called her "a pillar of the Detroit community and the passionate matriarch of the Detroit Lions football team."</p><p>Ford is credited with helping lift the Lions out of years of misery, being a pivotal figure in upgrading Ford Field and expanding the team's charitable and social-justice driven initiatives.</p><p>Bears chairman George McCaskey said in 2020 that his mother, Virginia McCaskey, and Ford were "very good friends." <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/02/06/virginia-mccaskey-bears-obit-dies-102-halas" >Virginia McCaskey died last year at 102</a>.</p>

entries.title: How Spencer Knight tries to aid Blackhawks' efforts to allow fewer odd-man rushes
entries.summary: <p>SEATTLE — The sound of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> goalie Spencer Knight banging his stick against the ice echoed through Calgary’s antiquated Saddledome late in the first period Saturday.</p><p>It wasn’t because a Flames player was about to exit the penalty box. Instead, it was because Knight noticed the Hawks getting too low in the offensive zone, a bad habit of theirs that often leads to odd-man rushes against.</p><p>Roman Kantserov and Wyatt Kaiser had led a rush up the ice, with Tyler Bertuzzi and Sam Rinzel forming a second layer. That left Frank Nazar as the only Hawks player behind the play. Knight hoped to alert one of the other four to drop back and join him.</p><p>The warning, in this case, didn’t help. When Rinzel flubbed his shot, the Flames quickly sprung a partial breakaway for Joel Farabee behind Nazar, forcing Knight to make a save.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Spencer Knight’s stick-banging didn’t prevent a Flames breakaway in this case: <a href="https://t.co/nevW84MngA">pic.twitter.com/nevW84MngA</a></p>— Ben Pope’s Video Clips (@BenPopeCSTclips) <a href="https://x.com/BenPopeCSTclips/status/2125393588611846404?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 25, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>But it’s the thought that counts, and Knight has made it his habit to bang his stick in those situations. He confirmed Tuesday he does it when ‘‘the ‘D’ dives down and there’s no one covering.’’</p><p>‘‘I don’t know if it makes a difference or not . . . [or] if it’s me just trying to be engaged,’’ Knight said. ‘‘If I see something, I do something.’’</p><p>He wasn’t sure anybody had noticed it, but I have seen it numerous times from up in the press box. Coach Jeff Blashill said he hasn’t noticed it behind the bench, perhaps because he’s trying hard to alert the skaters to the same issue.</p><p>‘‘I’m usually yelling,’’ Blashill said with a chuckle. ‘‘So [if] he’s banging his stick and I’m yelling, between the two of us, hopefully they can hear.’’</p><p>Last season, Hawks defensemen mentioned how Knight is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2025/12/11/blackhawks-spencer-knight-voice-blind-spot-detection-louis-crevier-defensemen" target="_blank" >unusually vocal</a> for a goalie. He lets them know when there’s somebody behind them who needs guarding, for example, or when they have enough time and space to skate with the puck.</p><p>Presumably, he’s still doing that. Plus, he now has found another way to communicate to the opposite end of the rink.</p><p>Whether because of Knight’s help or not, the Hawks have been more responsible lately about ensuring at least two men stay high in the offensive zone and on the forecheck.</p><p>‘‘We’ve done a much better job with our ‘F3’ reload and the decisions of when to go down walls and when not to,’’ Blashill said. ‘‘We want to be a pressure team . . . but there’s going to be times where the ‘D’ have to read they can’t [pressure]. And they’ve done a much better job of that — way better than where we were at two weeks ago.’’</p><p>That, in turn, gives Knight more support. In the Hawks’ recent 4-1-1 upturn, he has faced 7.5 high-danger shots per 60 minutes (according to Natural Stat Trick), down from 10.3 per 60 minutes before this stretch, which was the most in the NHL.</p><p>That has helped him record a .904 save percentage and plus-2.2 goals saved above average during this stretch, compared with his .881 save percentage and minus-3.5 GSAA before it.</p><p>The Hawks have <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/10/blackhawks-goalies-spencer-knight-arvid-soderblom-drew-commesso" target="_blank" >ridden Knight hard</a>, starting him in 19 of their 24 games so far — including all 13 home games. Only Wild goalie Jesper Wallstedt has made more starts than Knight leaguewide.</p><p>Blashill said the Hawks ‘‘monitor’’ goalies’ workloads in five-game segments. After new backup Drew Commesso finally started (and won) Sunday against the Canucks, however, it’ll be surprising if Knight doesn’t get the next three games.</p><p>Knight’s extremely disciplined off-ice health and recovery <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2025/11/30/blackhawks-nhl-goalie-spencer-knight-off-ice-habits-red-light-mat" target="_blank" >tactics</a> allow him to play a lot without getting mentally or physically fatigued.</p><p>Between games and practices, he’s adept at what he calls ‘‘turning off’’ his body and minimizing his energy burn, conserving his tank for the relatively few hours per day he needs to be ‘‘on.’’</p><p>‘‘That’s something I’ve worked on and gained and learned through experience,’’ Knight said.</p>

entries.title: White Sox to sign free-agent outfielder Tyrone Taylor to two-year contract
entries.summary: <p>Four prominent free-agent starting pitchers already have found new homes this week, including left-hander <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/11/24/cubs-trevor-rogers-mlb-offseason-free-agents-rumors-pitching-starting-rotation-2027" target="_blank" >Trevor Rogers</a>, whom the Cubs added late Monday. The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> still are searching for their own rotation upgrade.</p><p>On Tuesday, however, they checked a different item off their to-do list: right-handed outfielder. A source confirmed to the Sun-Times that the Sox have reached a two-year, $17 million agreement with Tyrone Taylor, with the deal expected to be announced officially next week.</p><p>Taylor, 32, is coming off a career-best season at the plate. He hit .279/.325/.502 with 11 home runs in 97 games with the Mets and Cubs, joining the latter in August as part of a trade that also brought right-hander Clay Holmes to the North Side.</p><p>With Randal Grichuk now a free agent after an excellent season facing left-handed pitching for the Sox, Taylor projects as a more defense-oriented replacement, potentially platooning with Sam Antonacci and Braden Montgomery in the outfield corners.</p><p>Taylor’s offensive game is known more for contact than power, but he did hit .318/.348/.574 against lefties in 2026, whereas Antonacci and Montgomery fared significantly better against right-handers.</p><p>A speedster with experience at all three outfield spots, Taylor should be an above-average defender in a corner role and has the strong throwing arm necessary to play in right field. Alongside center fielders Tristan Peters and Brenton Doyle, he could round out a strong Sox outfield late in games.</p>
entries.author: James Fegan

entries.title: Man fatally shot after argument at Brighton Park warehouse
entries.summary: <p>A man was fatally shot after an argument in Brighton Park Tuesday afternoon, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The 36-year-old man was in a warehouse in the 2600 block of West 35th Street at 3:33 p.m. when he got into an argument with another person who shot him, police said. The 36-year-old was taken to Mount Sinai Hospital where he later died.</p><p>A suspect has not been taken into custody, police said. The shooting is under investigation.</p>

entries.title: Illinois becomes sixth state to say no to Trump’s federal tax credit scholarship program
entries.summary: <p><i>This story was </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/11/24/illinois-governor-pritzker-says-no-to-trump-administration-federal-tax-credit-scholarship-program/" target="_blank" ><i><u>originally published by Chalkbeat</u></i></a><i>. Sign up for their newsletters at </i><a class="Link" href="http://ckbe.at/newsletters" target="_blank" ><i><u>ckbe.at/newsletters</u></i></a><i>.</i></p><p>Gov. JB Pritzker <a class="Link" href="https://gov-pritzker-newsroom.prezly.com/gov-pritzker-prioritizes-public-education-and-declines-trump-administrations-voucher-program" target="_blank" ><u>announced</u></a> Tuesday that Illinois won’t opt in to the federal tax credit scholarship program, making it the sixth state to reject the Trump administration’s initiative.</p><p>Pritzker, who won reelection for his third term as governor earlier this month, had kept quiet this year about whether he would elect to opt into the program. It allows individual taxpayers to receive dollar-for-dollar tax credits up to $1,700 for donations toward scholarship-granting programs that pay for tuition and other education services in private and public schools. His <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/10/13/illinois-advocates-split-on-pritzker-federal-education-tax-credit-decision/" target="_blank" ><u>decision came down to the wire</u></a>, as state leaders only have until the end of the year to join the program.</p><p>The governor’s office said participating in the program would be a detriment to <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/2025/12/09/federal-tax-credit-scholarships-enacted-by-trump-start-to-take-shape/" target="_blank" ><u>students who attend public schools</u></a>. Some public education advocates, including <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/08/27/chicago-education-advocates-call-on-pritzker-to-opt-into-federal-tax-credit-scholarship-program/" target="_blank" ><u>a sitting Chicago Board of Education member</u></a>, had called on the governor to opt in, arguing that public schools <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/2026/09/30/how-school-choice-federal-tax-credits-could-help-students-in-public-schools/" target="_blank" ><u>could fill budgetary gaps with the donations</u></a>. The governor’s statement also said he is wary of the lack of oversight for private school donations and how little say states have over <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/2026/10/02/federal-education-tax-credits-rules-pose-test-for-democratic-governors/" target="_blank" ><u>setting guidelines for the program</u></a>.</p><p>“At a time when public school education needs investments more than ever, we should not siphon money from public schools for private education – especially as the Trump administration’s policies decimate education,” Pritzker said in his statement. “We have a responsibility to do right by all of our students.”</p><p>Illinois lawmakers ended a <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2023/11/14/illinois-laws-voucher-scholarship-private-schools-end/" target="_blank" ><u>short-lived state tax credit scholarship program</u></a> in late 2023. It was set up in 2018 as part of broader school funding legislation that led to annual increases to public school districts.</p><p>Illinois taxpayers can still benefit from the federal rebates for education donations, but they can only make donations to groups that operate outside of the state. Pritzker’s decision means Illinois schools cannot receive money from the program.</p><p>The announcement puts an end to the intense debate among education advocates in Illinois over whether Pritzker should join the program. The Illinois Education Association and the Illinois Federation of Teachers, the state’s two largest teachers union, were vocally opposed to participating in the program.</p><p>Illinois <a class="Link" href="https://eftccredit.com/states" target="_blank" ><u>joins five other Democratic-led states</u></a> — Oregon, Minnesota, Arizona, Wisconsin, and Virginia — that have opted out of the program, which starts Jan. 1, according to an Education Freedom Tax Credit resource site. At least three Democratic governors have <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/2026/10/09/ny-gov-hochul-opts-into-federal-scholarship-tax-credit/" target="_blank" ><u>opted in</u></a>, while a handful of others were forced to participate after state legislatures overrode their decisions.</p><p><i>Makiya Seminera is a reporter covering how the state and federal government affect education in Chicago and across Illinois. Contact Makiya at mseminera@chalkbeat.org.</i></p><p><i>Chalkbeat is a nonprofit news organization </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/11/24/illinois-governor-pritzker-says-no-to-trump-administration-federal-tax-credit-scholarship-program/" target="_blank" ><i><u>covering public education</u></i></a><i>.</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/04/30/will-pritzker-opt-in-to-federal-program-that-covers-private-and-public-school-costs-these-advocates-hope-so" >Will Pritzker opt in to federal program that covers private and public school costs? These advocates hope so</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/01/28/pritzker-still-deciding-if-illinois-will-join-federal-program-that-funds-private-school-scholarships" >Pritzker still deciding if Illinois will join federal program that funds private school scholarships</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Ja'Dyn Lloyd leads Belleville West to an opening win and East Peoria's Cole Dubois scores 29 to beat Dunbar
entries.summary: <p>LINCOLN, IL — J’Dyn Lloyd has a direct line to Belleville West royalty. Lloyd, a current Belleville West senior and one of the state’s top players, is in regular contact with EJ Liddell, the Belleville legend who led the Maroons to back-to-back Class 4A state championships in 2018 and 2019.</p><p>“[Liddell] is one of the biggest role models in my life,” Lloyd said.</p><p>It isn’t hard to picture this year’s Belleville West squad playing in Champaign in March. Lloyd scored 24 points to lead the No. 15 Maroons past Danville 70-41 in the season opener on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-basketball/scores/2026/11/24/illinois-high-school-basketball-scores-chicago" >Tuesday</a> at the Lincoln/Eaton Thanksgiving Tournament.</p><p>Lloyd is strong and athletic, with natural scoring skills. He plays with an aggressive confidence on offense, something that has been lacking around the state lately. The 6-6 guard had five rebounds, four assists and three steals.</p><p>He scored eight points in Belleville West’s 17-0 second-quarter run to take control of the game.</p><p>The Maroons lost a starter, Caiden Capell, for the season due to a football injury, and several players in the rotation are experiencing varsity for the first time. But the group has size and talent.</p><p>Amauri Fenton, a 6-6 junior, had 20 points, five rebounds and four assists.</p><p>“First game we were just trying to get a feel for it on the court,” Lloyd said. “First half was a little risky, but we got the jitters out and played well in the second half.”</p><p>Senior guard TJ Cason, who has major college offers for track, threw down two blindingly athletic dunks and finished with eight points, eight rebounds, four steals and four blocks.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure entries.title: How Chicago's ballot petition challenges work and what it means for Mayor Johnson's candidacy
entries.summary: <p>Former state Sen. Rickey Hendon is leading efforts to remove Mayor <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/02/willie-wilson-petition-challenges-mayor-brandon-johnson-signatures-mayoral-election" target="_blank" ><u>Brandon Johnson</u></a> from the ballot on behalf of Willie Wilson, the millionaire businessman mounting his fourth mayoral campaign.</p><p>Candidates need 12,500 valid signatures to qualify for the Feb. 23 mayoral ballot.</p><p>Johnson submitted nearly 32,000 signatures, but Hendon is leading the charge <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/02/willie-wilson-petition-challenges-mayor-brandon-johnson-signatures-mayoral-election" target="_blank" ><u>to challenge</u></a> more than 25,000 of them.</p><p>The adjudication of challenges will continue until Dec. 17, when the final mayoral ballot is certified.</p><h3>Could Mayor Johnson really be knocked off the ballot?</h3><p>As of Nov. 23, Chicago Board of Elections officers recommended that more than <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/23/chicago-mayor-brandon-johnson-campaign-petitions-challenge-signatures-rickey-hendon-willie-wilson" target="_blank" >6,100 of Johnson’s signatures</a> be tossed. More than 2,200 were recommended to be upheld; another 8,600 were sent back for review.</p><p>At this rate, the incumbent mayor would still qualify for the ballot with more than 12,500 signatures.</p><p>Hendon had predicted Johnson would become the first incumbent Chicago mayor to be disqualified from the ballot.</p><p>But Johnson’s campaign manager, Christian Perry, said he is confident the mayor will survive the challenge.</p><h3>What happens if Johnson has less than 12,500 signatures?</h3><p>Johnson can still get on the ballot.</p><p>If the challenge takes the mayor under the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/10/26/chicago-mayoral-race-last-day-of-filing-mendoza-pappas-2027-election" target="_blank" ><u>required 12,500 signatures,</u></a> Johnson’s campaign could still get affidavits from people whose signatures were challenged to clear up any discrepancies. That would help the mayor meet the required number.</p><p>But even if Johnson’s name does appear on the ballot, the challenge will strain his <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/02/willie-wilson-petition-challenges-mayor-brandon-johnson-signatures-mayoral-election" target="_blank" ><u>campaign coffers</u></a>.</p><h3>What’s the problem with Johnson’s contested signatures?</h3><p>Hendon had a team of 20 people <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/23/chicago-mayor-brandon-johnson-campaign-petitions-challenge-signatures-rickey-hendon-willie-wilson" target="_blank" >scrutinizing Johnson’s petitions</a>.</p><p>Problems include photocopied signatures, missing addresses and people who live outside Chicago. There were also petitions that didn’t belong to Johnson’s campaign, Hendon said. For example, “Melissa Conyears-Ervin for treasurer was in there.”</p><h3>Are other candidates being challenged?</h3><p>Yes.</p><p>Wilson’s campaign has focused its challenges on Johnson and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/23/chicago-mayor-brandon-johnson-campaign-petitions-challenge-signatures-rickey-hendon-willie-wilson" target="_blank" ><u>Danielle Carter-Walters</u></a>, candidate for Chicago Flips Red, Hendon said.</p><p>Wilson’s campaign had also reviewed signatures for other candidates, including Cook County Treasurer Maria Pappas, outgoing Illinois Comptroller Susana Mendoza and Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias, the presumed front-runner.</p><p>But none of them had issues early in their signatures, Hendon said, so his team narrowed their scope to Johnson and Carter-Walters.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/10/26/chicago-mayoral-race-last-day-of-filing-mendoza-pappas-2027-election" target="_blank" ><u>Giannoulias’ campaign</u></a> manager Hana Jubeh last month said the presumed front-runner planned to scrutinize everybody’s nominating petitions and will use his $19.3 million campaign war chest to challenge anyone whose signatures appear shaky.</p><h3>How many candidates are running for mayor?</h3><p>There are <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/09/13/who-is-running-for-chicago-mayor-2027-election" target="_blank" ><u>16 mayoral candidates</u></a> as of Tuesday, but that will likely change.</p><p>Campaign managers and veteran political operatives said they expect the crowded mayoral field to shrink substantially as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/10/26/chicago-mayoral-race-last-day-of-filing-mendoza-pappas-2027-election" target="_blank" >candidates closely scrutinize</a> each other’s nominating petitions to make certain they have the required 12,500 valid signatures.</p><p>No one will be immune from those challenges.</p><h3>Have other incumbent mayors been challenged?</h3><p>Mayor <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/02/willie-wilson-petition-challenges-mayor-brandon-johnson-signatures-mayoral-election" target="_blank" ><u>Richard M. Daley</u></a>, Chicago’s longest-serving mayor, is the last incumbent to have his petitions challenged. To qualify for the 2007 ballot, Daley filed just 24,100 signatures, and his petitions were challenged, unsuccessfully, by rival candidate William “Dock” Walls.</p><p>But no incumbent mayor has been removed from the ballot, said the Chicago Board of Elections.</p><h3>Have candidates been removed from the ballot in the past?</h3><p>Yes. For example, veteran political consultant Frank Calabrese mounted the 2019 petition challenge that knocked mayoral candidate Dorothy Brown off the ballot. Brown had filed roughly 25,000 signatures.</p>

entries.title: Latino student drop drives CPS enrollment decline as many immigrant hubs grapple with rising costs
entries.summary: <p>Imelda Rodriguez has noticed fewer familiar faces at Irma Ruiz Elementary in Pilsen as the class that started kindergarten with her son has dwindled.</p><p>Enrollment at Ruiz fell by 45 students this year after seeing slight increases in 2023 and 2024 with the arrival of many migrant families. Rodriguez said it’s sad that her son has lost friends in his four short years at Ruiz.</p><p>“His classmates are not the same anymore, they all moved out,” Rodriguez said.</p><p>She wonders if “maybe they went to a better school,” but she and her son Remi, who is now a fourth grader, both like Ruiz and its surrounding community.</p><p>“I don’t know why they keep leaving,” Rodriguez said.</p><p>This year, enrollment fell in Chicago Public Schools by roughly 4%, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/09/24/chicago-public-schools-enrollment-drops-by-more-than-11-000-accelerating-long-term-downward-trend" target="_blank" ><u>hitting the lowest student count in more than two decades</u></a>. Latino enrollment fell by about 7,800 students, accounting for more than two-thirds of the districtwide decline this year, according to a <a class="Link" href="https://kidsfirstchicago.org/publications/cps-enrollment-fell-again-five-trends-that-explain-whats-changing" target="_blank" ><u>new report from the education nonprofit Kids First</u></a>.</p><p>Little Village, Brighton Park, Belmont Cragin and other predominantly Latino areas on the Southwest and Northwest Sides that have been hubs for immigrants experienced the steepest declines this year, according to the report. The Lower West Side, which includes Pilsen, also experienced a large decline, according to CPS. Meanwhile, enrollment has increased in pockets of the city, such as Kenwood, and in more affluent areas like O’Hare, the Near North Side and Lincoln Park.</p><p>Ruiz is among dozens of schools in Latino communities that have experienced significant drops in enrollment over the last 10-plus years and continue to shed students.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b70000" name="image-b70000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9bbab5e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5946x3337+0+45/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F65%2F3d%2F7726473e41ea84e92f6432316f25%2Fpilsenenrollment-261125-8.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8c8c9b2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5946x3337+0+45/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F65%2F3d%2F7726473e41ea84e92f6432316f25%2Fpilsenenrollment-261125-8.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bdd6545/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5946x3337+0+45/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F65%2F3d%2F7726473e41ea84e92f6432316f25%2Fpilsenenrollment-261125-8.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Remi Rodriguez, a student at Irma C. Ruiz Elementary School in Pilsen, stands outside the school after dismissal." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bdd6545/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5946x3337+0+45/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F65%2F3d%2F7726473e41ea84e92f6432316f25%2Fpilsenenrollment-261125-8.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1a79d8f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5946x3337+0+45/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F65%2F3d%2F7726473e41ea84e92f6432316f25%2Fpilsenenrollment-261125-8.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bdd6545/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5946x3337+0+45/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F65%2F3d%2F7726473e41ea84e92f6432316f25%2Fpilsenenrollment-261125-8.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Remi Rodriguez is in fourth grade at Ruiz Elementary in Pilsen. His mom has noticed how many of the kids who started school with her son in kindergarten have left.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Experts say the enrollment dips in these areas are <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2019/11/29/20913976/pilsen-schools-gentrification-enrollment-elementary-housing-whittier-cooper-walsh-ruiz-jungman-casas" target="_blank" ><u>linked to long-standing factors</u></a> that have intensified in recent years — such as high property taxes, an expensive housing market and rising costs of living — that make it more difficult for those with roots to stay and families with children to move in.</p><p>Many of the areas with the steepest enrollment declines this year were also <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/02/12/no-recess-lockdowns-less-learning-how-immigration-agents-disrupted-cps-schools-this-fall" target="_blank" ><u>hotspots for the federal government’s aggressive deportation campaign</u></a> last year.</p><p>Since the 2016-17 school year, Latino enrollment has fallen by 22%, or around 38,000 students. At Ruiz in Pilsen, enrollment dropped by 48%, or 372 students in the same span.</p><p>While funding for individual schools isn’t as directly tied to enrollment as it was in the past, how many students a school has can impact what it offers, such as sports teams and other extracurricular activities. Schools with few students can also become targets for closure. In 2013, the district used low enrollment as a metric to identify <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2023/06/16/after-closing-50-schools-in-2013-did-chicago-keep-its-promises" target="_blank" ><u>which schools to shutter.</u></a></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-930000" name="html-embed-module-930000"></a><div style="min-height:521px" id="datawrapper-vis-lvRkd"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/lvRkd/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-lvRkd"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/lvRkd/full.png" alt="Chicago Public Schools 20th day enrollment" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Many factors that contribute to declining enrollment are out of the district’s control. Mirroring national trends, fewer children are being born in the city, which means fewer kindergartners are entering CPS. Families are also having fewer children than in previous decades.</p><p>The cost of living in certain parts of Chicago is also a factor.</p><p>There are far fewer affordable units that rent for $900 or less a month in the Lower West Side than there were a decade ago, according to Geoff Smith, executive director of DePaul University’s Institute for Housing Studies. In 2024, 15% of available units for rent in the community area were affordable, down from 73% in 2010, according to the research center’s analysis.</p><p>Home prices have also increased, making it more difficult for some families to find homes they can afford. The typical homebuyer in Pilsen last year made around $170,000 a year — up significantly from the $114,000 they made in 2019. Between higher interest rates and escalating property taxes, a higher income is essentially a must to purchase a place.</p><p>On top of that, developers have been purchasing two- and three-flat buildings and converting them into single-family homes, reducing the total housing stock in the area.</p><p>At the same time, fewer families with children are calling Pilsen home. In 2010, 37% of Pilsen households had children compared to 30% citywide, Smith said. Fast forward to 2024 and just 21% of Pilsen households have kids, compared to 23% across Chicago.</p><p>Smith said this could mean that as it became more expensive to live in Pilsen, families without children were the ones who could afford to move in — “a key driver of enrollment.” But he noted that the decline could also include families whose children started in CPS and left.</p><p>Pilsen lost the most Latinos from 2010 to 2023, <a class="Link" href="https://uofi.app.box.com/s/9gstad2axqipfbop894huqs0p2vnqdqg" target="_blank" ><u>according to a recent report</u></a> from the University of Illinois Chicago’s Great Cities Institute on the shifting makeup of longstanding Latino neighborhoods. And the broader Lower West Side recorded lower rates of Latino home ownership than other areas of the city.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-c70000" name="image-c70000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/72a7ab1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6182x3469+0+350/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc1%2Fa1%2F11ddd1ac4442b416b910cc1a5896%2Fpilsenenrollment-261125-7.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e1d2101/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6182x3469+0+350/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc1%2Fa1%2F11ddd1ac4442b416b910cc1a5896%2Fpilsenenrollment-261125-7.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/32e197c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6182x3469+0+350/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc1%2Fa1%2F11ddd1ac4442b416b910cc1a5896%2Fpilsenenrollment-261125-7.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="A sign for Irma C. Ruiz Elementary School in Pilsen." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/32e197c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6182x3469+0+350/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc1%2Fa1%2F11ddd1ac4442b416b910cc1a5896%2Fpilsenenrollment-261125-7.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/984ac35/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6182x3469+0+350/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc1%2Fa1%2F11ddd1ac4442b416b910cc1a5896%2Fpilsenenrollment-261125-7.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/32e197c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6182x3469+0+350/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc1%2Fa1%2F11ddd1ac4442b416b910cc1a5896%2Fpilsenenrollment-261125-7.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Patricia Mota attended Ruiz Elementary as a child when the school was bustling with children. When she got elected to the Local School Council, she saw how much her beloved school had changed.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Patricia Mota doesn’t need to see the statistics to know there are fewer children in Pilsen.</p><p>Mota grew up in the neighborhood and graduated from eighth grade at Ruiz in 2008, when the school had more than twice its current enrollment. At the time, the school was large enough to stage elaborate renditions of works like “Fiddler on the Roof,” Mota remembers, and she spent her summers exploring the neighborhood with other kids her age, often crowding around ice cream trucks for a cool treat.</p><p>“Summer breaks were crazy here,” Mota said.</p><p>In 2020, Mota ran for and won a seat on Ruiz’s Local School Council, a role she filled until this summer. She realized that things had changed at her beloved school.</p><p>The school still stages performances, but they are pared down. And there’s now less getting to know “families who are different from your own,” Mota said.</p><p>“I think there were 100 kids in my eighth grade class, so you got more connections, more interactions with different kids,” Mota said.</p><p>A similar trend is happening in Gage Park. At Gage Park High School, enrollment this year fell below 300 students for the first time. Enrollment at the school has dropped by 84% since 2010.</p><p>Joel Rodriguez, a community organizer with the Southwest Organizing Project, which works with schools and families on the Southwest Side, said he’s noticed the exodus of families from the area. He blames rising housing costs, safety concerns and low job availability.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-1c0000" name="html-embed-module-1c0000"></a><div style="min-height:508px" id="datawrapper-vis-gOfHI"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/gOfHI/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-gOfHI"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/gOfHI/full.png" alt="Gage Park High School enrollment has plummeted since 2010 (Line chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Rodriguez thinks the city needs a comprehensive strategy that tackles all those issues to attract more families.</p><p>“Families want a place where they can see their children growing up, where there's real opportunities to thrive,” Rodriguez said.</p><p>Some Latino families are settling down elsewhere to find that. Growth among that population is “increasingly occurring beyond historic Latino centers, including Austin, Garfield Ridge, Chicago Lawn, Ashburn, Clearing, and West Lawn,” the Great Cities report states.</p><p>But experts say many of these families likely ended up in the suburbs where homes can be more attainable.</p><p>Ivan Arenas, associate director at the Institute for Research on Race and Public Policy at the University of Illinois Chicago, says areas outside of Cook County are increasingly popular landing spots for Latino families.</p><p>The number of Latino residents in the collar counties, such as McHenry, DuPage, Kane and Lake, doubled in size between 2000 and 2023. The number of Latino residents in Cook County also increased during that time, but at a slower rate, Arenas said.</p><p>When Mota walks around Pilsen with her family now, she can’t help but notice one building in particular. It looks the same as it did when she was a kid, but the family that lived there is gone.</p><p>“It's a weird sensation,” she said, “because you hold all the memories of the people that used to live here.”</p>

entries.title: Jackson Park's 'Gold Lady' shines again thanks to $1 million renovation
entries.summary: <p>The last time Jackson Park's Gold Lady statue truly looked gold, the Sears Tower was the world's tallest building — can you believe it's ranked No. 25 now? — Millennium Park didn't exist and the biggest show in town was Michael Jordan's flying circus, playing to rave reviews and championship rings at the United Center.</p><p>But check out the Statue of the Republic now — especially in the morning, when sunlight hits the east-facing 24-foot sculpture at 63rd Street and Richards Drive.</p><p>The work absolutely glistens again, thanks to a $1.1 million regilding project that wrapped up this month.</p><p>"It's a magnificent upgrade for the Gold Lady," Chicago Park District Director of Historic Assets Andrew Schneider said. "She [sends] out resplendence across Jackson Park, as she did when she was first dedicated 108 years ago."</p><p>Working behind enclosed scaffolding, a crew of specialists spent about four months removing the sculpture's flaking gold leaf, repairing the bronze statue's surface, then hand-applying 25,000 gossamer-thin pieces of gilt.</p><p>The last regilding happened in 1993 and that was the first time the statue had been recoated since it was erected in 1918.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a Hayes Dr.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Schneider said park officials estimate the current tone will last 50 years, helped along by a gold colored primer that will become visible as the gilded surface fades.</p><p>The Statue of the Republic was designed by Daniel Chester French, a sculptor whose large body of work includes the Sitting Lincoln sculpture at Washington, D.C.,'s Lincoln Memorial.</p><p>Henry Bacon, the architect who oversaw the design and engineering of the Lincoln Memorial, created the statue's 10-foot base.</p><p>Wearing a tunic, a laurel crown and holding an eagle-topped globe in her right hand and a staff inscribed with the word “liberty” in her left, the statue honors the centennial of Illinois' statehood — and the 25th anniversary of the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, which was held in Jackson Park.</p><p>For French, the sculpture marked a return trip to Jackson Park. The work is a smaller version of the original Statue of the Republic, a 65-foot colossus that overlooked the exposition's Court of Honor and its Administration Building.</p><div class="Enhancement" Both statues were intended as tributes to the ideals of the still-young nation.</p><p>But French's original statue and most of the exposition's major buildings were temporary structures made of plaster. They were destroyed after the fair. </p><p>Indeed, the old South Parks Commission got rid of the Republic by burning her down.</p><p>The exception was the Palace of Fine Arts, which was constructed with a brick substrate, allowing the building to be renovated and reopened as the Museum of Science and Industry in 1933.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-2f0000" name="image-2f0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a09fe04/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7d%2F5b%2Fa53cb4934f00aaeabd66e65658ae%2Flady-261125-5.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/15bd849/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7d%2F5b%2Fa53cb4934f00aaeabd66e65658ae%2Flady-261125-5.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a377a96/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7d%2F5b%2Fa53cb4934f00aaeabd66e65658ae%2Flady-261125-5.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="The recently regilded Statue of the Republic at Jackson Park. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a377a96/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7d%2F5b%2Fa53cb4934f00aaeabd66e65658ae%2Flady-261125-5.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e5f1a5f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7d%2F5b%2Fa53cb4934f00aaeabd66e65658ae%2Flady-261125-5.JPG 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a377a96/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7d%2F5b%2Fa53cb4934f00aaeabd66e65658ae%2Flady-261125-5.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>The recently regilded Statue of the Republic at Jackson Park. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>"The original monument was just such a massive piece and such a major focal point for the fair," author and Chicago parks historian Julia Sniderman Bachrach said. "To think how much this meant to Chicagoans 25 years later. [What better way] to commemorate that whole period — that whole moment in Chicago — of the [original] statue."</p><p>The regilding made some of the statue's details more visible, such as a breastplate bearing an armored eagle, Bachrach said. And although it's nearly impossible to see from the ground, French carved his initials near the statue's collar.</p><p>The Art Institute of Chicago’s B.F. Ferguson Monument Fund covered the $140,000 cost of the gold leaf, according to a museum spokesperson.</p><p>Schneider said the Park District next wants to renovate the sculpture's base but will need to find the money to do it.</p><p>"Because it's probably going to exceed twice the cost of the gilding," he said.</p>

entries.title: 9 ‘Nutcrackers’ to help kick off the holiday season in Chicago
entries.summary: <p>“Nutcracker” season is underway, and a Chicago icon is helping to put a fresh spin on an old classic.</p><p>Rapper and West Side native <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/11/24/da-brat-hip-hop-nutcracker-chicago-music-rap-history-lgbtq-holiday" target="_blank" ><u>Da Brat</u></a> is an MC of “The Hip Hop Nutcracker," which runs through Nov. 29 at Cadillac Ranch Theatre.</p><p>In a recent interview with the Sun-Times, the radio co-host, author and performer said she is looking forward to providing some nostalgia for the adults, introducing hip-hop to the kids and providing a good time for all in a chaotic world.</p><p>“I just want people to enjoy themselves and be in the holiday spirit,” she said. “We need to be entertained.”</p><p>The production is just one of many “Nutcracker”-themed productions opening this week and next in the city and surrounding suburbs. From Joffrey Ballet’s classic production to "Nutcracker on Ice” to a presentation of Duke Ellington’s jazzy take on Tchaikovsky’s score, there is truly something for all tastes. Read on to learn about nine of this year’s festive programs.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" Palace Theatre, 151 W. Randolph St.<br><b>Info:</b> Tickets are $52.85 - $187.30; <a class="Link" href="http://broadwayinchicago.com" target="_blank" ><u>broadwayinchicago.com</u></a></p><p>“The Hip Hop Nutcracker” is one of the most unique “Nutcracker”-themed dance presentations of the bunch this year. Instead of ballet, audiences will witness the magic of breaking and other forms of hip- hop dance. Tchaikovsky’s score is remixed with DJing and rapping, courtesy of both Da Brat and music icon Kurtis Blow, who burst on the scene in 1979 with the hit “Christmas Rappin’.” The family-friendly production has some of the same story beats and characters from the original “Nutcracker” tale, but the setting is a spirited, graffiti-covered New York City instead of the 19th century.</p><div Southport Ave.<br><b>Info:</b> Tickets are $22 - $59; <a class="Link" href="http://aacenterfordance.org" target="_blank" ><u>aacenterfordance.org</u></a></p><p>A&A Ballet’s “Art Deco Nutcracker” transports furry mice, a dancing dragon and party guests in Art Deco gowns to Chicago during the Roaring Twenties. The production may have a lot of glitz, but the choreography by A&A Ballet co-founder Alexei Kremnev is classical ballet.
