entries.title: Bears and Lions: a Thanksgiving mega-matchup that's truly delicious — and long overdue
entries.summary: <p>DETROIT — Three things I think I know about the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>, who are all set to take on the Lions in a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/24/bears-lions-detroit-chicago-picks-predictions-odds-pointspread-thanksgiving-thursday-nfl-ford-field" target="_blank" >Thanksgiving showdown of NFC North co-leaders</a>:</p><p><b>1. They’re “thanks”-worthy — and the Lions are, too — for a change: </b>Who could forget the first of the Bears’ and Lions’ 20 head-to-head matchups on Thanksgiving, back in 1934? Goodness, how exciting. The Bears were 11-0. The Lions were 10-1. America gathered in front of the TV and … wait, no TVs? Never mind.</p><p>The matching 8-2 records aren’t quite as pristine in meeting No. 21, the rivals’ 14th Turkey Tussle since the NFL started televising these games, but it’s only the second time in the TV era — and the first since 1991 — both teams come in with winning records. And that makes this one a gift to behold.</p><p>Generally speaking, Bears-Lions on Thanksgiving has been as appetizing as thick-skinned gravy ladled out of an old shoe. When the Bears have been good, the Lions have been bad. When the Bears have been bad, the Lions have been good. The exceptions being those times both the Bears and Lions have been bad, otherwise known as most of the time.</p><p>You’ve probably redacted it from your memory, but your 2021 self actually sat there in a semi-catatonic heap and watched the 3-7 Bears and 0-9-1 Lions waste three and a half hours together before Bears kicker Cairo Santos walked off a not-at-all-epic 16-14 win with a short field goal at the gun. Then-coach Matt Nagy, rumored to be toast at game’s end, would survive another handful of weeks before being fired into the sun.</p><p>And in 2024, you watched Caleb Williams and the 4-7 Bears storm back from 23-7 down against the 10-1 Lions and have a chance to win or at worst tie, trailing by three inside of a minute and on the edges of field-goal range. Cue mismanaging Matt Eberflus, who froze on the sideline, leaving his rookie quarterback and team to die an unspeakable death as the clock struck zeroes. Eberflus was canned the next day.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Thanksgiving history: Matt Eberflus final call as a head coach…<br><br>I still can’t believe we let him coach Caleb Williams <a href="https://t.co/tc3wavIAjK">pic.twitter.com/tc3wavIAjK</a></p>— ChicagoPainNetwork (@ChicagoPainNet) <a href="https://x.com/ChicagoPainNet/status/2125328397312082234?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 24, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>What a pleasure it is to have a big — no, huge — Bears-Lions matchup instead of that nonsense.</p><p>The last time the teams faced a Thanksgiving game that even compared, it was 1991 and the Bears roared in at 9-3. But the upstart Lions — 8-4 and amid their first winning season in nearly a decade — won 16-6. Mike Ditka, quite the character, if you didn’t know it, ripped his players as being unfocused and called their six-point effort a “copout.”</p><p>More of these games have been duds like the 1979 rendition. The Bears were a perfectly decent 7-5, but the Lions were a pathetic 1-11. On CBS’ pregame show, household-name handicapper Jimmy “The Greek” Snyder rated the Bears as better at virtually every position and said, “Chicago is an exciting team today. The Lions are in trouble.” Final score: Lions 20, Bears 0.</p><p>At least on this occasion — a fine one, indeed — there’s every reason to expect to be highly entertained.</p><p><b>2. They’re better off being the road team: </b>It might seem like the Bears would have a better chance at Soldier Field than Ford Field, but consider the Lions’ 1-8 record in their last nine Thanksgiving games (all at home). Coach Matt Campbell is 1-4.</p><p>“That comes with any team that plays at home on a holiday weekend or holiday game,” Campbell said. “A lot of our guys, most of our guys — coaches, too — they’ve got family [in town]. You got your own kin, then you’ve got your significant other’s … [and] the hard thing is you don’t want to say no, right? That’s where it gets tricky. You’re trying to entertain and so it’s hard to just tell somebody, ‘Look, I’ve got stuff I’ve gotta do.’ ”</p><p><b>3. They’re still the Bears, though: </b>And what that continues to mean, among other things, is losing games within the division. Forget about Thanksgiving games — the Bears have dropped seven of the last eight overall against the Lions, and the most recent one in Detroit, last September, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/09/15/terrible-backwards-quite-embarrassing-bears-52-21-loss-to-lions-was-tough-for-85-team-to-watch" target="_blank" >was a 52-21 bludgeoning</a>. Which team bucks its negative trend?</p><h3><b>Caleb-o-meter: 5 out of 10</b></h3><p>In the space of two games — both of them wins, mind you — Williams has gone from the fringes of the MVP conversation to the struggle bus. It doesn’t take much to knock a young QB down a couple of pegs.</p><p>But a big Thursday — buoyed by pleasant childhood memories of watching Thanksgiving football with his dad while plowing through his mom’s homemade spinach dip by the gobful — could bring the good vibes right back.</p><p>“Now, I get to be a part of making memories for somebody else,” he said. “So we want to go out there and put on a show and have fun doing it.”</p><h3><b>Look who’s coming: the Lions</b></h3><p>The Bears ride in on a five-game winning streak — one shy of their hosts’ six in a row.</p><p>Lions QB Jared Goff is playing the “best football of his career,” according to Bears coach Ben Johnson, who used to be Goff’s offensive coordinator and would know.</p><p>But the key to the whole operation for the Bears’ defense is keeping running back Jahmyr Gibbs, the NFL leader in yards from scrimmage, from stealing the show like the great Barry Sanders did in 1997 when he rushed for 167 yards and three touchdowns in a 55-20 Thanksgiving mauling of the Bears. What, you’d forgotten that masterful performance already? Come on, it wasn’t even three full decades ago.</p><h3><b>Three and out</b></h3><h3></h3><p><b>The Big 3-0-0: </b>Williams sits tied with Mitch Trubisky for the most 300-yard passing games (seven) by a Bears QB in his first three seasons. As for which golden-armed slinger is better, we’ll leave that tough call to you.</p><p><b>Wu, that’s who: </b>The halftime act at Ford Field will be hip-hop group Wu-Tang Clan, whose original members include Method Man, Ol’ Dirty Bastard and Ghostface Killah. But you knew that already.</p><p><b>Thanks for nothing: </b>The Bears’ next opponent after the Lions? The Jaguars, the only NFL team never to play on Thanksgiving.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/24/bears-lions-detroit-chicago-picks-predictions-odds-pointspread-thanksgiving-thursday-nfl-ford-field" target="_blank" >Bears predictions: Week 12 at Lions</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/24/bears-dandre-swift-ben-johnson-fumbles-running-back-hold-ball-nfl-kyle-monangai-salvon-ahmed" >After another fumble, what do Bears do with D’Andre Swift now?</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/24/bears-qb-caleb-williams-looks-to-get-back-to-goldilocks-zone-in-potential-shootout-with-lions" >Bears QB Caleb Williams looks to get back to Goldilocks Zone in potential shoot-out with Lions</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams has been more like Jared Goff — and that's a good thing
entries.summary: <p>The day that the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> introduced Ben Johnson as their head coach in January 2025, Caleb Williams positively beamed. He'd coveted Johnson, having watched his offense — and his quarterback — from afar.</p><p></p><p>Johnson was going to build the Bears’ offense from the ground up, not make a navy-and-orange replica of what he’d done in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/24/bears-qb-caleb-williams-looks-to-get-back-to-goldilocks-zone-in-potential-shootout-with-lions" target="_blank" >Detroit</a>. That excited Williams.</p><p></p><p>“Not every player is Jared Goff,” Williams said that day, “but you’re yourself.”</p><p></p><p>In his third year, though, Williams is as close as ever to being Goff. And that’s a compliment.</p><p></p><p>When the two face off at Ford Field on Thursday in one of the Bears' most consequential Thanksgiving games ever, Williams will continue stating his case as a pocket passer. His head coach’s mandate for 70% completion percentage from Williams is no coincidence — Goff completed 72.4% of his passes in their last year together before Johnson took the Bears’ job.</p><p></p><p>This year, the Lions quarterback fifth in passing yards, eighth in passing touchdowns and fourth in passer rating. He’s completed 67.8% of his passes.</p><p></p><p>Williams, though, has completed 68.3%.</p><p></p><p>Williams, when he’s at his efficient best, is doing what Goff does — getting the ball to his receivers in stride so they can knife up the field. What's unique is his ability to use his speed when plays break down.</p><p></p><p>Goff doesn’t have that option, though he did scramble for an uncharacteristic 10-yard run in Sunday’s win against the Buccaneers. What he does in the pocket has been worth Williams’ years-long studying.</p><p></p><p>“He’s always done well with getting the ball out when it’s time, and delivering the runner ball,” Williams said. “And he’s got guys that go and make plays. So, same thing over here.”</p><p></p><p>Goff sees the defense well, Williams said, and has benefited from head coach Dan Campbell and new offensive coordinator Drew Petzing — the former is Johnson’s mentor, the latter a former groomsman in Johnson’s wedding — keeping a version of Johnson’s offense.</p><p></p><p>“He knows it like the back of his hand,” Williams said. “When the shots are there, he takes them, he alerts them. When it’s not he’s checking the ball down, living to fight another down — and I think that’s playing quarterback. I think playing quarterback is being able to manage the game and manage the situations throughout the whole game. It’s not just in the fourth quarter … I think he does a really good job of that.”</p><p></p><p>Williams was a fourth-quarter maestro last year. He’s been more consistent throughout the game this season — the Bears haven’t trailed in five full games. His first three games after returning from injury was among one of the best stretches in franchise history. Williams was the first Bears quarterback ever to, in a three-game stretch, post a total passer rating over 110, throw no interceptions and win three times.</p><p></p><p>In his past two games, though, Williams has thrown four touchdowns and five interceptions — and posted a 72.9 passer rating. Coach Ben Johnson claimed Tuesday he’d “kinda flushed Sunday” already before giving a lukewarm review, saying Williams was “solid” against the Saints.</p><p></p><p>“As an offense, we've really been stressing the ball security part of it ..'" Johnson said. “We can't gift them anything in that regard.”</p><p></p><p>Williams has thrown six interceptions in seven games. Goff has thrown four in 10.</p><p></p><p>“He's playing the best football of his career as far as I'm concerned,” Johnson said of Goff. “He does a great job taking care of the football, highly accurate, and of course he's got great playmakers around him.”</p><p></p><p>Receivers Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jameson Williams are in the top-20 in receiving yards and top-10 in receiving touchdowns. Tight end Sam LaPorta is eighth in receiving yards among tight ends. And running back Jahmyr Gibbs is the favorite to be the NFL’s Offensive Player of the Year. Those players all developed with Johnson in charge.</p><p></p><p>“[Johnson] had a very good vision for football and concepts and detail,” Campbell said. “I’ve always knew something was in there with him. I always thought it was impressive. I’m just fortunate to have the time that we have together.”</p><p></p><p>Johnson is 0-2 against his mentor as a head coach. The last time he went to Ford Field, he lost by 31.</p><p></p><p>The stakes are different, though, than they were in Week 2 of last season. Both teams are 8-2; the winner takes first place of the NFC North with six weeks to play.</p><p></p><p>“This is how they drew it up when the schedule rolled out,” Goff said.</p><p></p><p>The Lions haven’t lost a game since Oct. 4, the Bears since Oct. 11.</p><p></p><p>“This is the good stuff,” Campbell said. “This is the stuff that gives you all the tinglies.”</p>

entries.title: 2026 Chicago Sun-Times All-Public League football team
entries.summary: <p>Two years ago, Lawrence Carr was a backup wide receiver in his first year at Kenwood after transferring from Mount Carmel, wishing for more playing time.</p><p>‘‘I was kind of mad that I wasn’t getting in,’’ Carr told the Sun-Times.</p><p>Then, at the end of the first half of a game against St. Francis, one of the Broncos’ receivers had to take a breather.</p><p>‘‘Lawrence was standing there when I said, ‘We need a receiver,’ ’’ Kenwood coach Chris Goffer told the Sun-Times.</p><p>So Carr went into the game, quarterback AJ Crooms hit him on a post route and he was off to the races for a touchdown on his first varsity play. It was a sign of things to come.</p><p>Now Carr is the top uncommitted senior in the state, a three-star prospect with almost 20 Division I offers. He is also one of four Kenwood players named to the Sun-Times’ All-City team, which was selected by the Chicago Public League Football Coaches Association.</p><p>Carr said he expects to pick a college in the next six weeks or so. In the meantime, he has one more high school game to play. Kenwood (8-4), which beat Lane 27-13 last week for the Public League title, plays Catholic League champ Leo (7-5) in the Prep Bowl in Friday. Kickoff is scheduled for 11 a.m. at Rockne Stadium.</p><p>Playing with three quarterbacks in three seasons, Carr has emerged as ‘‘a consistent staple in our offense,’’ Goffer said. This season, the speedy 5-11, 170-pounder has 39 catches for 1,036 yards and 12 touchdowns.</p><p>Carr has come a long way from the days when he first got into football as a kid running around Avalon Park on the South Side.</p><p>‘‘We’d run around the track, do skills work on every position,’’ he said.</p><p>Carr was a quarterback in youth football before switching to receiver when he got to Mount Carmel. He’s a natural at the position, Goffer said.</p><p>‘‘He’s got some of the best ball-tracking skills I’ve ever seen at the high school level,’’ Goffer said. “[And] he’s just got some grown-man hands. The sky’s the limit for Lawrence. He’s definitely a Power Four kid.’’</p><p>Kenwood and Morgan Park, which won the regular-season Public League title, lead the All-City team with four players each.</p><p>Joining Carr from the Broncos are senior running back Jamarius Andrus, senior offensive lineman Elijah Thomas and sophomore defensive back Rashard Warfield.</p><p>Morgan Park’s All-City players are junior quarterback Ronald Smith Jr., senior receiver Travezz Jones, senior linebacker Milen Porter and senior defensive back Darrell Mattison.</p><p>King has three picks: senior running back Herman Yancey, senior offensive lineman Cornelius Moore and senior linebacker Paul Norman.</p><p>Four teams had two representatives each: Westinghouse (junior athlete Ethan Wiley and senior linebacker Daesean Gafford), Simeon (senior offensive lineman Kayden Jordan and senior defensive lineman Corey Randolph Jr.), Lane (senior defensive lineman Kanye Williams and senior kicker/punter Atticus Whitted) and Perspectives (junior defensive lineman Kobe Hamlet and senior defensive back Dicaprio Turks).</p><p>Rounding out the team are two senior offensive linemen — UIC Prep’s Kavon Grant and Goode’s Ryan Ogburn — and Payton senior defensive lineman Kobe Ferguson.</p><p>The All-Public League football team is selected by the Chicago Public League Football Coaches Association.</p><h3>2026 All-Public League First entries.title: Police seek suspect in strong-arm robbery aboard Red Line train in Englewood
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police are seeking a man suspected of robbing and assaulting a passenger aboard a CTA Red Line train in Englewood earlier this month.</p><p>The robbery happened around 12:37 a.m. Nov. 9 while the train was near the 63rd Street station in the 200 block of West 63rd Street, according to a community alert from police.</p><p>The suspect approached another passenger, took items the person's pocket and punched the passenger as he exited the train, police said.</p><p>The suspect is described as a Black man about 20 years old, 5-foot-10-inches tall and 160 pounds. He was last seen wearing black pants, a black jacket and a white hoodie underneath, police said. In the photo released by police, the man also has a goatee and is wearing white athletic shoes with black markings.</p><p>Anyone with information is asked to contact Mass Transit Detectives at 312-745-4447 or submit an anonymous tip at CPDTIP.com using reference number JK482722. </p>

href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydkddljy-l-i/" target="_blank" >Today’s ‘teen takeovers’ are yesterday’s moral panics</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydkddljy-l-d/" target="_blank" >Mary Norkol</a></h5><h5></h5><p><b>Getting together</b>: It starts with a hastily made flyer on social media naming a time and place. Then it snowballs into hundreds of young Chicagoans, mostly teenagers of color, gathering to hang out with friends. The teens have a good time and then head home. Neighbors may be irritated, police may keep an eye on them, but the gathering is little more than an inconvenient disruption.</p><p><b>At issue</b>: Sometimes, these gatherings end in tragedy. One year ago, a teen boy was killed and eight others were wounded in a shooting at a so-called "teen takeover" downtown. A few years before that, another teen boy was shot and killed during a similar gathering in the same place. Now the gatherings, even the nonviolent ones, draw judgment and outcry from adults around Chicago and the suburbs.</p><p><b>Past and present</b>: To the Chicago History Museum's Greg Storms, the response reflects past moral panics — and the strained relationship young people and adults have always had. Very few elements of these gatherings are new, except maybe the scale. Social media and other technology have allowed these unofficial, often disorganized gatherings to grow by the hundreds.</p><p><b>Go deeper</b>: Reporter Mary Norkol examines Chicago's history of "teen takeovers," digging into how race plays a role in the way gatherings are perceived and past trends of "wilding," "Punkin' Donuts" and social demonstrations, spanning the 1970s to 1990s. <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydkddljy-l-k/" target="_blank" ><b>Read more here</b></a><b>.</b></p><p><b>Listen up</b>: Mary also joined Mary Dixon and Patrick Smith on >Chicago’s must-try Puerto Rican restaurants</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydkddljy-l-tr/" target="_blank" >Ambar Colón</a></h5><p>For her latest, Sun-Times arts and culture reporter Ambar Colón pulled from her family's list of go-to Puerto Rican restaurants from when she was growing up and tried some newer spots in the city.</p><p>The result is an essential list of six old-school and new Puerto Rican restaurants worth visiting for anyone who knows the cuisine well or is looking to try their first dish. Though she couldn't cover everything, these are some of her picks:</p><p><b>Borinquen, 3811 N. Western Ave.</b></p><p>Juan "Peter" Figueroa "invented" the jibarito at Borinquen in the 1990s, using flattened and fried plantains to replace sandwich bread the same way people in Puerto Rico have done for years. Division St.</b></p><p>The best time to eat at La Bruquena is on a Friday or Saturday night, when the restaurant hosts live music. While you're there, get the mofongo stuffed with shrimp, served with chicken broth.</p><p><b>Jibaritos on Harlem, 3317 N. Harlem Ave.</b></p><p>If you want to try or re-experience Chicago Puerto Rican food, this is the place. Besides solid dishes like mofongo, bistec encebollado and (of course) the jibarito, this spot also has a great brunch menu with Puerto Rican-inspired dishes such as guava pancakes, tostón toast and the jibarito breakfast burger.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydkddljy-l-ty/" target="_blank" ><b>FULL LIST HERE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>Where do you now, or where did you meet up with old pals when everyone's back in town for the holidays? entries.title: U.S. stockpile of bomb-making chemical lead azide to be detonated Wednesday morning at Iowa plant, Army says
entries.summary: <p>Middletown, Iowa — The U.S. Army plans to detonate the nation’s entire stockpile of lead azide in Iowa at 9 a.m. Wednesday, warning that the dangerously degrading bomb-making chemicals could otherwise explode at any time.</p><p>“Inaction is no longer an option,” said Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, the Army’s leader of the operation.</p><p>Officials on Tuesday warned nearby residents to be ready to evacuate to avoid toxic dust in the air while also trying to assure them that barriers around the blast zone should limit much of the plume.</p><p>“We don’t believe that the public should be in a panic,” said Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle. “Our goal is to keep as much of it as we can here on our Iowa Army Ammunition plant to prevent it from traveling.</p><p>The controlled detonation of roughly five tons of degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown has set off concerns about potential health and environmental effects and frustration over a lack of information. Experts have advised the stockpile will become more volatile as temperatures cool in the coming days.</p><p>The Army rescheduled the detonation in southeastern Iowa to Wednesday because of more favorable wind conditions and to allow more time for extra safety measures, according to the court filing by the government.</p><p>Detonation of the 68 barrels had been set for last Friday. The Army said they need to blow up the stockpile to prevent a possible chain-reaction explosion, which would be more dangerous.</p><h3>Army takes steps to limit plume</h3><p>Officials overseeing the plan say the wind on Wednesday is expected to blow southwest, away from nearby Burlington, a city of nearly 25,000 people along the Mississippi River.</p><p>The Army released new maps Tuesday showing the likely trajectory of the plume traveling toward Missouri. Plans for an earlier detonation had the plume headed north and possibly west into Illinois.</p><p>An emergency notification sent to cellphones Tuesday morning said the detonation was planned for 9 a.m. Wednesday and that some people within 5 miles southwest of the plant may be evacuated.</p><p>The “imminent threat alert” told those up to 20 miles away to remain indoors with windows closed “to avoid airborne lead dust, noise and vibration.”</p><p>The Army has set up additional “blast barriers” around the bunkers where the lead azide will be detonated, and to apply ballistic gels and foams to absorb the lead dust. It also plans to douse the materials with thousands of gallons of water.</p><p>“We’ve taken every viable solution and considered it,” Telle said. “In every instance, the answer is controlled detonation is safest.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-180000" </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Laura Bargfeld/Associated Press</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Federal court approved the detonation</h3><p>The Army won approval for the detonation from the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in a saga that sowed confusion and included an unusual twist from President Donald Trump. </p><p>A court said Monday that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency adequately incorporated safeguards in an emergency permit to minimize the dispersal of dust. Those conditions address the concerns of environmental groups that sued to stop the detonation, the court said.</p><p>The court pointed to barriers put up around the area where the barrels are stored along with weather restrictions.</p><p>The judges said the record also reflected that the Army evaluated “a full range” of alternatives, including using other chemicals to neutralize the lead azide and thermal treatment but determined detonation was safest.</p><p>In an twist, Trump, commander-in-chief of the Army, said in a social media post that besides court approval, he wanted Gov.-elect Rob Sand to OK the detonation. Sand, a Democrat who doesn’t take office until January, has said the decision is fully up to the Trump administration.</p><h3>Blast was planned for last week</h3><h3></h3><p>The Army has changed the detonation date three times following an outpouring of public concern.</p><p>Environmentalists sued last week to stop the detonation at the site, about 90 miles south of Cedar Rapids. The court temporarily halted the permit, prompting the Army to argue it didn’t need authorization after all, given that it was an emergency.</p><p>An attorney for the environmentalists emphasized their legal challenge centers on the validity of the EPA permit, not the Army’s decision to move forward with the detonation under the emergency provision.</p><p>Earthjustice managing attorney Rachel Rintelmann said the lawsuit has alerted the public to the threat. Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds activated the state emergency management office on Friday. The state also created a website for information about the operation.</p><p>Reynolds said Tuesday that, after speaking with military leaders, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, she supports the planned detonation.</p><p>“I trust the Army will do everything in its power to protect the people who could be affected,” Reynolds said. “And we will make sure the state is fully prepared to support the effort to keep Iowans safe. To that end, I have asked the Army for additional information that will allow my team to best prepare for Iowa’s pre- and post-detonation response and have been assured it will be provided."</p><h3>Residents in limbo ahead of detonation</h3><p>Some residents near Middletown have been sealing windows and doors to keep out any lead dust from the detonation. Others living farther away were raising concerns about the possible paths the plume could take depending on the wind.</p><p>Officials have recommended that people stay indoors when the detonation happens and clean off outdoor surfaces with water afterward to limit exposure to any lead particles.</p><p>Middletown Mayor Rodney Johnson said the detonation must take place “so we can move on with our lives.”</p><p>“Improper storage and disposal is where things go wrong,” he said on social media.</p><p>Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe said state agencies are working to establish additional monitoring of air and water quality, public health and agriculture resources.</p><h3>Army says plans intended to avoid something worse</h3><h3></h3><p>In court filings, Army Col. Aaron Teller, a munitions emergency response specialist, said that less liquid inside the barrels means the solution is more susceptible to freezing, which increases the risk of an explosive chain reaction.</p><p>Staff at the Iowa ammunition plant notified the EPA about the barrels in March. The Army then assembled experts in munitions chemistry, engineering and environmental safety to come up with a plan.</p><p>According to EPA documents, alternatives to a detonation were considered. But officials said handling the drums would increase the probability of an accidental, fatal blast.</p><p><i>Contributing: Associated Press writers Konstantin Toropin in Washington, D.C.; Scott Bauer in Madison, Wisconsin; Jacques Billeaud in Phoenix; Christopher Weber in Los Angeles and Dave Collins in Hartford, Connecticut. Montoya Bryan reported from Albuquerque, New Mexico.</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/11/20/the-army-plans-to-detonate-a-toxic-lead-compound-near-the-illinois-iowa-border-heres-what-to-know" >The Army is about to detonate a toxic lead compound near the Illinois border: Here’s what you need to know</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/11/23/trump-orders-the-army-not-to-detonate-bomb-making-chemicals-in-iowa-without-court-approval" >Federal appeals court clears way for U.S. Army to detonate degraded bomb-making material in Iowa</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Our swinging acquaintance lied to us about not being married
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My husband and I have been married for 32 years. We have been happy, but we decided to spice things up by starting a swinging lifestyle. We only play together and have met some nice people.</p><p>We have known a man, "Roger," for two years and have had some nice threesomes. We state in our profile that we don't want to help a spouse cheat. We had this conversation with Roger on our first meeting, and he told us he was divorced.</p><p>Well, it's come to our attention that he lied. He's married and has been using me (and other women) as a way to cheat. I'm disgusted. My question is, do we tell Roger's wife what he is doing? He seems to have no guilt. What do we do? — <i>SOUTHERN PLAYGIRL</i></p><p><b>DEAR PLAYGIRL:</b> I'll assume you've stopped sleeping with Roger. Your responsibility ends there. Roger's cheating is between him and his wife, and I wouldn't be surprised if she already has some inkling of his activities. Either way, you aren't the marriage police, you don't know what's going on in their relationship, and it's none of your business.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My husband and I own a vacation place that has become his obsession. If he could, he would live there 100% of the time, and he's become a pest, trying to convince everyone to spend time there. Honestly, the only reason anyone ever goes there is to make him happy. If it were up to me, I would never set foot in the darned place ever again, but every year I find myself giving in.</p><p>The last straw was when we had not one but two deaths in the family. At the time of the first one, he was on his way to his place and didn't even consider canceling his plan. For the second, I'm staying at our primary home because we lost someone very close to me, but he's already talking about going to his place the day after the funeral. I'll probably give in and go with him.</p><p>I've considered leaving him after all the years together if that's the most important place in the world for him. He can have it; I'm old enough to enjoy the rest of my life. I know I sound selfish and shallow, but enough is enough! — <i>ME OR THE HOUSE</i></p><p><b>DEAR M.O.T.H.:</b> Instead of leaping straight to divorce, why not learn to say no? Stop giving in, but don't let it turn into a fight. If he wants to sulk about having to go by himself, so be it. He needs to learn that he's the only one who loves that other house.</p><p>Give him free rein to spend as much time in his happy place as he wants. If you decide you miss him, you can always accompany him or drop in for a visit from time to time. If the time apart becomes a serious problem for either of you, you may want to involve a licensed family therapist ... or a lawyer.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>
entries.author: Abigail Van Buren

entries.title: Lawmakers, snap into action for those who can’t feast this Thanksgiving
entries.summary: <p>Every family has their own traditions for a Thanksgiving menu. It could start with classics like turkey and stuffing, or maybe you skip turkey altogether and focus on the sides. There might be secret recipes passed down through generations, or dishes from ancestral homelands. In my opinion, you can’t go wrong when you have good food and good people.</p><p>This is the fun of planning Thanksgiving dinner. But for too many families this year, putting a menu together involves a different kind of planning — whether they can afford a meal at all.</p><p>The cost of a basic meal, let alone a holiday feast, is simply out of reach for thousands of households across the Chicago area. Our neighbors are facing impossible choices. Food or medicine? Groceries or gas? How do we stretch what’s left in the refrigerator until the next paycheck clears?</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-1c0000" name="module-1c0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>A recent <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagosfoodbank.org/2026-hunger-in-chicago-report/" target="_blank" >survey</a> conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago found that 31% of Chicago households had to delay or skip payment on a basic need like medicine, housing or utility bills so they could afford food. </p><p>In July 2025, the federal government enacted HR1, more commonly known as the so-called “One Big Beautiful Bill," cutting a projected $200 billion from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, our nation’s most important anti-hunger program.</p><p>As the Sun-Times' Elvia Malagón <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/11/19/snap-enrollment-in-illinois-keeps-dropping-in-wake-of-one-big-beautiful-bill-overhaul" >reported</a> last week, the consequences of these SNAP cuts are becoming more dire as each month passes. </p><p>In Illinois, approximately 450,000 people have lost SNAP benefits since July 2025 — a 24% decrease. They are children, older adults, people with disabilities, veterans and hardworking families — not numbers on a data table. Every day they fall further behind as the cost of living rises and the federal safety net is torn apart.</p><p>The average monthly SNAP benefit isn’t enough for a fancy holiday meal with all the fixings. But it’s still a critical lifeline that helps keep basic groceries in the kitchen. Without SNAP, more neighbors are turning to local food pantries or skipping meals altogether.</p><p>Food banks and pantries across Chicago and Illinois are working tirelessly to meet these growing needs, but we cannot replace SNAP. We were never intended to shoulder the responsibility of feeding entire communities. Historically, for every one meal a food bank provides, SNAP provides nine.</p><p>The future of SNAP is in grave danger. As a result of HR1, the federal government plans to end its 62-year responsibility for covering the entire cost of SNAP benefits and will require states to pick up a significant portion of the tab. Beginning in October 2028, Illinois could be on the hook to pay as much as $428 million annually or risk losing SNAP altogether. This is a significant and unprecedented financial obligation for our state at a time when more families are struggling to afford their most basic needs.</p><p>We cannot allow disastrous policy decisions in Washington, D.C., to be the reason families in Chicago and across Illinois go hungry. It doesn’t have to be this way.</p><p>Congress can and should act immediately to delay the new SNAP cost-shifting requirements. Then they should pursue every opportunity to reverse all harmful changes made through HR1, including all cuts to SNAP and Medicaid.</p><p>Illinois leaders also have an important role to play. We need our state to use every tool at its disposal to ensure people who are eligible for SNAP can access and remain enrolled in the program. And state lawmakers must begin preparing now to protect the program for a day when cost-shifting takes effect.</p><p>For those of us who are lucky enough to gather around the table and share a meal, I hope we take a moment to remember the hundreds of thousands who are worrying about whether they’ll have enough food to go around.</p><p>We cannot control the circumstances every family faces. But we can stand up and protect the programs designed to help them.</p><p>This Thanksgiving, let’s remember that putting food on the table shouldn’t be a privilege in this land of plenty. It should be a guaranteed basic human right. Please contact your members of Congress and your state legislators and urge them to protect SNAP.</p><p><i>Kate Maehr is executive director and CEO of the Greater Chicago Food Depository.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-7b0000" name="module-7b0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>
entries.author: Kate Maehr

entries.title: A Thanksgiving reminder: Don't let old grievances keep you from family
entries.summary: <p>Thanksgiving is upon us, and many Americans are preparing to gather around tables laden with turkey, stuffing and trimmings. It also means that many are bracing for the familiar familial fault lines: old grievances, unresolved resentments, siblings who won't speak with each other and the parent or child whose absence is as conspicuous as the empty chair at the table.</p><p>For all its Norman Rockwell promise of togetherness, Thanksgiving can be a painful reminder of the distance between the families we have and the families we wish we had.</p><p>The Bible knows a thing or two about dysfunctional families. If the blame game were an Olympic sport, the sibling rivalry between Jacob and Esau would take the gold, with a record-breaking performance in finger-pointing, fault-finding and family dysfunction.</p><p>The trouble begins before the twins are born. Their rivalry is foretold while still in their mother Rebecca's womb. Esau emerges first, Jacob a close second, grasping his brother's heel. Their father, Isaac, favors Esau; Rebecca, favors Jacob. Jacob exploits his brother's hunger, trading a bowl of lentil stew for Esau's birthright. Years later, Rebecca engineers a deception in which Jacob impersonates Esau and tricks their blind father into giving him the blessing intended for his brother. Esau vows to kill Jacob. Jacob flees. A family is torn apart.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b80000" name="module-b80000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>Whose fault is it? Jacob, for his deception? Esau, for his impulsiveness and murderous threats? Rebecca, for her favoritism? Isaac, for his passivity? Even God, who foretold the brothers' rivalry before their birth?</p><p>There is no shortage of suspects. But perhaps we are asking the wrong question. Not whose fault it is, but who cares whose fault it is?</p><p>Of course, fault matters. Actions have consequences. Betrayal demands accountability. But at a certain point, what purpose is served by rehashing old injuries and revisiting the question of who did what to whom?</p><p>The Bible’s patriarchs and matriarchs' stories speak to us because of their humanity — their flawed family dynamics, missteps and misjudgments, frailties and failings, all mirrored in our own lives. As a congregational rabbi, I find myself less interested in the wrongs committed by Jacob and Esau than in the greater tragedy of the 20 years that followed — two decades of estrangement, silence and separation before the brothers would finally meet again.</p><p>During those years, both brothers marry, become fathers and build families. Children are born, joys and sorrows are experienced without a brother to share them. The tragedy is not simply what happened between Jacob and Esau. It is everything that never happened because of it.</p><h3>Ambiguous loss</h3><p>Their experience isn't an uncommon problem. <a class="Link" href="https://www.karlpillemer.com/books/fault-lines/" target="_blank" ><u>Research</u></a> conducted by Cornell University gerontologist Karl Pillemer found that 27% of American adults reported being estranged from at least one family member.</p><p>Unlike death, family estrangement often involves what psychologists call "ambiguous loss." There is no funeral, no clear moment of closure. The person is gone from your life but remains present in your thoughts. An open wound, flaring up at birthdays, weddings, holidays and other milestones. And the pain rarely stops. It ripples through entire families, separating grandparents from grandchildren, cousins from cousins, one generation from the next.</p><p>The causes are sometimes obvious: money, inheritance, in-laws, divorce. But often they are more subtle: unmet expectations, accumulated disappointments, a lifetime of perceived slights. We carry assumptions about how relatives should show up for our life events, including moments of need. When they fall short, disappointment hardens into resentment, then recrimination, and ultimately, rupture. No birthright has been stolen, but we feel cheated all the same.</p><p>Pillemer's research offers hopeful insight. Among those who reconciled, many stopped insisting that the other person accept their version of past hurts. Two people of good will can experience the same events and remember them differently. The absence of consensus about yesterday need not foreclose the possibility of a shared tomorrow.</p><p>When Jacob and Esau finally reunite, something remarkable happens, as significant for what does not happen as for what does. They do not relitigate the past. There is no dramatic confession, no apology or insistence that one acknowledge the other's account. Instead, the brothers embrace and weep.</p><p>The night before their reunion, Jacob wrestles with a mysterious adversary who pleads, “Let me go, for dawn has broken.” Jacob initially refuses. The symbolism is unmistakable. From the moment he emerged from the womb grasping his brother's heel, holding on is what Jacob does. Only when Jacob releases his grip, does he receive a new name: Israel. He could only become his fullest self when he finally learned to let go. He emerges wounded, walking with a limp, but capable of moving forward. Scarred, yet capable of becoming whole.</p><p>British Jewish novelist and playwright Israel Zangwill once wrote, “It takes two men to make one brother.” With Thanksgiving a day away, the pitfalls and possibilities of our families stand in plain view. Each one of us is empowered to decide whether we will rehearse old grievances or make room for new memories. We cannot change the past, nor can we compel another person to change. We can, however, choose what we hold on to and what we let go.</p><p><i>Rabbi Elliot Cosgrove is senior rabbi of Park Avenue Synagogue in New York City and author of “For Such a Time as This: On Being Jewish Today.” Cosgrove, who earned his Ph.D. from the University of Chicago Divinity School, previously served at Anshe Emet Synagogue in Lake View.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-eb0000" name="module-eb0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>
entries.author: Rabbi Elliot Cosgrove

entries.title: SNL's 'Sister' skit both funny and sad in highlighting caregiver challenges
entries.summary: <p>From the minute the "Saturday Night Live" sketch “Sister" — a fake ad about a 24/7 family caregiving solution that's "completely free and also <i>your</i> sister" —aired, millions of caregivers, particularly women, and their families saw a reflection of their own lives.</p><p>As a social worker for the Caring for Caregivers program at Rush University System for Health, I see this dynamic all the time: One daughter or son taking care of an aging parent, with little or no help from the rest of the family.</p><p>Within days, the video went viral. At the National Alliance for Caregiving’s Caregiver National Summit last week, nearly every conference session discussed the "SNL" sketch and the problems it spotlights.</p><p>The sketch was both funny and sad because it reveals a serious truth: Family caregivers of older adults, often women, face a difficult, overwhelming task, even when it’s a role they want to fulfill and one that they may find rewarding and meaningful. The work is so demanding and draining that caregivers often neglect their own health.</p><p>In the sketch, Kenan Thompson’s character says his sister doesn’t seem confused by the many medications she has to give to their dad.</p><p>“If she does, she hasn't brought it up to me, because I haven't asked.” </p><p>When you come together for Thanksgiving or other family gatherings, please ask how your family caregiver is doing. Ask them, “How much sleep are you getting? When was your last doctor’s appointment? When was the last time you had a day off?”</p><p>Offer to help in a concrete, useful way, by suggesting things you could do, like coming over so the caregiver can step out for a walk or to see a friend.</p><p>We've heard from family caregivers who said the sketch made them feel “seen.” This is their chance to be heard. Have a frank talk with your siblings, parents and other family members.</p><p>Let’s make this the start of an honest and ongoing conversation so caregivers and family members can share the load. You can learn more from <a class="Link" href="https://aging.rush.edu/caringforcaregivers/" target="_blank" >Caring for Caregivers</a> at Rush, <a class="Link" href="mailto:Caregivers@rush.edu" target="_blank" >Caregivers@rush.edu</a>, and 312-563-0350, as well as from Illinois' <a class="Link" href="https://ilaging.illinois.gov/forprofessionals/areaagenciesonaging.html" target="_blank" >list of Area Agencies on Aging</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://ilaging.illinois.gov/programs/caregiver/caregiver-wellness.html" target="_blank" >Caregiver Wellness</a> program.</p><p><i>Stephanie Bailey, licensed clinical social worker, and program coordinator, Caring for Caregivers, Rush University System for Health</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-e30000" name="module-e30000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Boys, men are among sexual abuse victims</h3><p>On Thanksgiving, families across Chicago will crowd around tables. Somebody will carve the turkey. Somebody will argue about the Bears. And at a lot of those tables, a man will be sitting with a secret he has never said out loud.</p><p>I know because for years, I was that man.</p><p>I was sexually abused as a boy. When I spoke up, my abuser threatened to kill me. So I learned what too many abused boys learn: Keep your mouth shut if you want to live.</p><p>Silence didn't make the abuse go away. It came out as habitual lying, a reckless sex life, and hardest to admit, jealousy of my own children.</p><p>I'm not rare. One in 6 men report being sexually abused, and most boys never report at all. Here at home, the Chicago Children's Advocacy Center responded to <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagocac.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/FY25-Annual-Report-Web-12.22.pdf" target="_blank" >1,903 investigative reports</a> in fiscal year 2025 — 1,463 of those involved sexual abuse allegations. The danger usually isn't a stranger. It's someone who gets invited to dinner.</p><p>Those boys become men taught to handle pain alone. In 2024, only <a class="Link" href="https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/products/databriefs/db564.htm" target="_blank" >10.9%</a> of U.S. men got counseling or therapy, compared with 16.9% of women. Men die by suicide at nearly four times the rate of women. That's not toughness. That's a slow funeral.</p><p>Three truths broke my silence: I was worth loving. It wasn't my fault. And my children needed a whole father, not a fragmented one. Shame is a liar.</p><p>So, Chicago, here's my ask.</p><p>If you're a man carrying this, tell one safe person before the year ends. If you're in crisis, call or text 988.</p><p>If you're a parent, grandparent, aunt or uncle, notice who wants time alone with the kids. Tell your sons that if anyone hurts them, you will believe them. If you suspect abuse, call the Illinois Department of Children and Family Services hotline at 1-800-25-ABUSE.</p><p>If you lead a church, a barbershop or a team, make room for men to talk.</p><p>Every broken boy and broken man desires to feel seen, safe and heard. Somewhere in this city, a boy is deciding whether it's safe to tell. Let's make sure the answer is yes.</p><p><i>Robert H. Marshall Jr., author, "Shame Is a Liar," and founder, The Survivors Circle and Echoes</i></p><h3>Gratitude for patient motorists </h3><p>This Thanksgiving, I'd like to acknowledge the patient and courteous drivers who stop their vehicles to let an elderly white-haired lady cross a busy four-lane street where there is no traffic light.</p><p>That lady is me, and while I don't condone the actions of these drivers (for their own safety), I always marvel at this incredible display of kindness. Quite a few drivers smile and blink their headlights to let me know it's safe to cross the street. I reciprocate with a little bow of the head and a wave of genuine thanks.</p><p>We are but passing ships in the night, and I think of these courteous drivers as kindred travelers who don't mind pausing for just a moment to acknowledge a stranger's preciousness and worth.</p><p><i>Kathleen Melia, Niles</i></p><h3>Tired tricks </h3><p>For many years, Donald Trump has been referring to Joe Biden as<a class="Link" href="https://www.the-independent.com/bulletin/news/trump-sleepy-joe-falls-asleep-oval-office-b3058494.html" target="_blank" > “Sleepy Joe.”</a> I once heard actor and comedian Mel Brooks say <a class="Link" href="https://www.phillyburbs.com/story/opinion/columns/2011/05/08/rewards-being-mocked/17899994007/" target="_blank" >“We mock the thing we are to be.”</a> Need I say more?</p><p><i>Eileen Carney, Palos Heights</i></p>

entries.title: It's (almost) Thanksgiving. What are you grateful for?
entries.summary: <p>You won the lottery.</p><p>You do know that, right? Start with that initial splash of "seminal wet," to use Walt Whitman's memorable phrase (one of several he coined for this particular substance. I smile to see Whitman included among Donald Trump's proposed National Garden of American Heroes. He wouldn't include Harvey Fierstein. It's because these Republicans don't read. "Leaves of Grass" could be titled "Tales of the City, 1855." It's a gay romp, in places).</p><p>Sorry, where was I? A hundred million sperm in a teaspoon of fatherstuff, to again cite Whitman, where only one — the future you — fought its way past all the others. A mad, tail-wriggling sprint over a few inches — still quite a distance for a tadpole 1/500th of an inch long. The equivalent of an adult swimming several miles. </p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-660000" name="module-660000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>Had another wriggled faster, you would have never existed, and some other, different person, at least genetically, would have taken your place. You would have ended up ... nowhere.</p><p>Instead, you beat 100 million-to-1 odds by just showing up, and since then have, through a combination of skill, smarts, and plain dumb luck, avoided the daily winnowing. You did not join those kindergartners blundering dreamily in front of a school bus. Or those high schoolers who chug 12 beers and drive into a tree. Or the sophomores surrendering to despair. Or adults who bite the baited hook of disease and are yanked out of this world long before their time.</p><p>Thanksgiving is Thursday. The emphasis is usually on what we are given. A luscious holiday feast, for starters, that most enjoy through the efforts of others. To the general bounty of our lives the other 364 days a year. Days that begin with glorious orange and yellow sunrises, the dawn breaking clear, then progress punctuated by colorful birds and strong cups of hot coffee. All the way to golden sunsets. Then the stars come out, twinkling emissaries from the past. The moon was full Tuesday night, the same moon that Julius Caesar, George Washington and Elvis Presley contemplated.</p><p>There is so much to give thanks for.</p><p>An odd word, "thank" — look it up in the Oxford English Dictionary, and its roots disappear a thousand years ago into Middle English and Teutonic, tangled with the word "think."</p><p>That's apt. Thankfulness is bound up in thought. It's an attitude, though we obscure that by giving thanks for specific benefits — for this good dinner, for that compliment, for being passed the stuffing — so much so that we forget that gratitude is also a philosophy, a general condition, an overarching mindset, the face we turn toward the world, no matter what expression the world is showing us at the moment.</p><p>Gratitude is not based on what you have. Rather it's the dog you hunt with. You unleash gratitude, say, "Go get 'em, boy," and see what he brings back, twitching. You must scan the woods for reasons. It takes effort. I remind myself, in the morning, to find something to be grateful for today. Even realities that at first seem something to complain about rather than appreciate. Growing old comes to mind. And my body falling apart. Not fun, but then, my friend Tony will never grow older than he was last year. And my friend Jeff's body fell apart in one crash in Michigan. Honestly, I'll take the slow version of both, and be grateful for them, as privileges denied many.</p><p>I recommend you do the same. Whatever ride you are on, it took the universe 13.8 billion years to cough you up into consciousness, and untold billions will pass after you snap off like a popped light bulb. Might as well enjoy it. And gratitude is the key to the door of happiness.</p><p>I know of an organization whose members are often in a state of disarray. Their personal lives are a miserable mess. They've torched their relationships. Wrecked their health, traded the glorious bounty of the world for staring into the outhouse hole of various addictions. And now even those are rudely denied them.</p><p>Yet they regularly speak of gratitude, for the small spark of a good life they've set among wet tinder and are huffing on with all their might. For whatever good is going on, and if none comes to mind, for the hope of better days to come. Gratitude is the rope they're tossed, and they grab at it.</p><p>So this Thanksgiving, whoever you are, I extend to you a lifeline. Whether or not you take it, well, I'm grateful for you considering the offer, and for you reading this today and throughout the year. I'm on vacation next week, finishing a book, but I've got one more column Friday, and am thankful for that, too. Happy Thanksgiving.</p>
entries.author: Neil Steinberg

entries.title: 2 passengers injured when small plane from Chicago area crashes near Louisville
entries.summary: <p>A small passenger plane that took off from far south suburban Lansing crashed in a residential area outside Louisville Tuesday afternoon after its pilot reported engine failure while approaching a Louisville airport, authorities said.</p><p>The pilot, operating a single-engine Beechcraft Bonanza A36 plane, was approaching Bowman Field Airport when he reported engine failure to air traffic controllers moments before the crash, according to recordings of communications with the Louisville control tower.</p><p>"I'm not going to make the field," the pilot told Louisville Air Traffic Control operators. "If I'm going into the house, I'll try to avoid anything I can."</p><p>The plane came down in Strathmoor Village, a suburb east of Louisville, where the pilot managed to avoid hitting any homes or other property, said Louisville Fire public information officer Capt. Jalen Green.</p><p>"The pilot did an outstanding job avoiding any property," Green said. "He hit the top of the trees, the canopy, and that slowed them down and put it right in the middle of the street."</p><p>The two people aboard the plane were taken to a Level 1 trauma center at University of Louisville Hospital. One suffered life-threatening injuries, while the other sustained serious injuries, Green said.</p><p>Louisville Fire crews arrived at the scene within three minutes of the crash, which was reported at about 2:40 p.m., according to Louisville Metro Emergency Services.</p><p>A dog was also aboard the plane and was in good condition and in the care of Louisville Metro Animal Services, Green said.</p><p>The identities of the two passengers have not been released. A Federal Aviation Administration incident report released Wednesday listed the plane as registered in far south suburban Lynwood, just south of Lansing.</p><p>The FAA and the National Transportation Safety Board are investigating.</p>
entries.author: Christiana Freitag

entries.title: Administración de Trump coloca monitores de tobillo a más inmigrantes, esto mantiene ansiosa a una residente de Chicago
entries.summary: <p>Últimamente, Liz se ha despertado de golpe por la noche, presa del pánico, cuando su monitor de tobillo comienza a vibrar. El zumbido le recuerda su mayor temor: que agentes de inmigración irrumpan en su pequeño apartamento en el lado norte de Chicago y se la lleven a un centro de detención.</p><p>"Los agentes de ICE me dijeron que el monitor vibraría si se rompía o si se manipulaba", dice ella entre lágrimas. "Nos buscarán de inmediato", cuenta que le dijeron, "porque sabemos dónde encontrarte".</p><p>La solicitante de asilo guatemalteca ha vivido en un estado constante de ansiedad desde que ella, su esposo y su hija fueron citados para una verificación migratoria inesperada el pasado agosto. Su esposo fue detenido por inmigración mientras a Liz le colocaron un monitor de tobillo y la dejaron en libertad junto con su hija de 15 años. Ni ella ni su esposo tienen antecedentes penales.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-6e0000" name="module-6e0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>WBEZ no está usando sus nombres completos porque temen represalias del gobierno.</p><p>"Le pregunté a los agentes de inmigración, '¿Por qué? ¿Hicimos algo malo?'", dice Liz, y agrega que desde que la familia llegó a Estados Unidos en 2024 de Guatemala han tratado de seguir al pie de la letra cada paso del proceso de solicitud de asilo.</p><p>Como Liz, más de 53,000 no ciudadanos en todo el país han sido equipados con monitores de tobillo en 2026 bajo el programa de Alternativas a la Detención del Departamento de Seguridad Nacional (DHS), según datos gubernamentales. Ese número se ha más que triplicado desde 2024, a medida que la administración de Trump ha intensificado la aplicación de la ley migratoria.</p><p>Es la misma tendencia a nivel local, encontró un análisis de WBEZ/Sun-Times. Hasta ahora este año, la oficina regional de ICE en Chicago —que supervisa Illinois, Indiana, Wisconsin, Missouri, Kentucky y Kansas— ha emitido casi 3,800 monitores de tobillo, un aumento de casi el 40% desde 2024.</p><p>El aumento ha generado preocupación entre defensores de inmigrantes por el impacto en la salud mental que, dicen, provoca la vigilancia constante en quienes llevan el dispositivo y no representan ningún riesgo. Los defensores sostienen que el uso de monitores de tobillo debe ser una alternativa a la detención, pero a medida que más personas han sido equipadas con ellos, también han aumentado las detenciones.</p><p>"Hemos visto a tantas personas en todo el país que han cumplido con sus casos migratorios, que tienen familias, que tienen trabajos, que tienen fuertes lazos con la comunidad, sin antecedentes penales significativos, que van a sus citas regulares y de repente los ponen con monitor de tobillo", dice Lauren Hodges, abogada principal del Amica Center for Human Rights, un grupo de defensa legal.</p><p>Defensores como Hodges señalan que la tendencia al alza comenzó poco después de una directiva interna de la administración de Trump el año pasado que ordenó a los agentes de inmigración poner monitores de tobillo a no ciudadanos "cuando sea posible."</p><p>Su organización presentó una <a class="Link" href="https://acrobat.adobe.com/id/urn:aaid:sc:US:4d60693e-0c67-40a7-85d7-6ed671007d97" target="_blank" >demanda colectiva</a> que acusa a la administración de Trump de exigir a no ciudadanos a llevar un monitor de tobillo o de muñeca sin justificar por qué se justifica una vigilancia tan "dañina e invasiva". La demanda dice que las personas con los dispositivos han sufrido problemas de salud como resultado, como hipertensión, así como ansiedad y depresión.</p><p>DHS no respondió preguntas específicas sobre su mayor uso de monitores de tobillo ni a otras preguntas sobre este dispositivo de rastreo. En un comunicado, la agencia defendió el programa ATD como una herramienta crítica para asegurar "el cumplimiento de las condiciones de liberación y las verificaciones regulares".</p><p>La agencia dice que las personas sin riesgo de fuga ni antecedentes penales se inscriben porque es la forma más "económica" de garantizar el cumplimiento con sus procedimientos migratorios.</p><h3><b>Efectos en la salud mental</b></h3><p>Alternativas a la Detención se inició hace más de 20 años como una manera de hacer seguimiento a inmigrantes que eran liberados bajo supervisión mientras enfrentaban la deportación.</p><p>Pero los defensores dicen que la vigilancia continua es solo otra forma de detención.</p><p>Cuando la administración de Trump les retiró a los haitianos el Estatus de Protección Temporal (TPS) en junio —lo que les había permitido a cientos de miles de inmigrantes que huían de desastres naturales o conflictos políticos en su país permanecer y trabajar temporalmente en EE.UU.— muchos de ellos fueron luego equipados con monitores de tobillo.</p><p>Entre ellos estuvo Pierre Damas Bel, un estudiante universitario y destacado jugador de fútbol. Informes noticiosos dicen que luchó profundamente con la humillación que le causaba el dispositivo, incluso compartiendo sus frustraciones en redes sociales antes de quitarse la vida.</p><p>Liz y su familia también han sufrido vergüenza y ansiedad por el dispositivo. En esa verificación de agosto, Liz dice que los funcionarios de inmigración debatieron abiertamente poner un monitor de tobillo a su hija de 15 años, aunque las pautas federales restringen al ICE de colocar dispositivos de rastreo a menores.</p><p>Al escuchar a los agentes, la adolescente, que juega flag football, comenzó a llorar. Temía ser acosada en la escuela o ser percibida como una criminal.</p><p>"Cuando vi su carita y empezó a llorar, me dijo: 'Mami, ya no voy a poder jugar más'".</p><p>Al final, los agentes dejaron a la joven sin monitor.</p><p>Desde entonces, dice Liz, la vergüenza de llevar un monitor de tobillo ha sido devastadora. Ajustado con fuerza a su pierna, el dispositivo es voluminoso e incómodo.</p><p>"Cuando voy a la iglesia me gusta ponerme falda o vestido, y ahora no puedo", cuenta. "Tengo que ponerme un vestido largo para que la gente no me mire. Es vergonzoso".</p><p>"Estamos criminalizando el hecho de ser inmigrante", dice Jennifer Babaie, subdirectora del Adult Detention Project en el National Immigrant Justice Center. "La mayoría de las personas que están siendo arrestadas son gente que está solicitando [estatus] o que de otro modo tiene un estatus legal... ahora estás con un monitor de tobillo, y de repente entras en una categoría completamente distinta".</p><p>No sólo más personas llevan monitores de tobillo, sino que los llevan por más tiempo.</p><p>ICE ha impuesto cada vez más monitores de tobillo con GPS a inmigrantes incluso después de que jueces federales han ordenado su liberación de custodia porque el gobierno no pudo justificar la detención, dijo Anthony Enriquez, vicepresidente de defensa y litigio del Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, durante un reciente panel dirigido por el periodista de datos Austin Kocher.</p><p>Los defensores de derechos humanos sostienen que la política federal sobre monitores de tobillo no es necesaria y está impulsada por la crueldad y por las ganancias que obtienen las empresas que suministran los monitores. El costo de la tecnología pasó de aproximadamente $25,500 al día en 2022 a más de $145,000 en 2026.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure Actualmente estudia inglés.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Ansiedad constante de que el monitor falle</b></h3><p>Liz dice que su familia siempre ha estado bajo alguna forma de vigilancia federal. A su esposo le colocaron un monitor de tobillo cuando llegó por primera vez a Estados Unidos en 2024. Aun así, la familia logró encontrar trabajo y construir una vida en Chicago después de huir de la violencia y la delincuencia en las calles de Guatemala. Él trabajó como recolector de chatarra y ella limpiaba casas.</p><p>Ahora Liz intenta mantener a la familia por su cuenta.</p><p>Pero está navegando.</p><p>A fines de octubre, Liz recibió un mensaje inesperado que le ordenaba presentarse a una verificación migratoria en el mismo edificio donde arrestaron a su esposo. Temía que los agentes la acusaran de manipular su monitor y la detuvieran.</p><p>"Vengo preparada para cualquier cosa, porque no sé qué podría pasarme adentro", dice.</p><p>En la mañana de su cita, la abogada de Liz no pudo asistir, así que ella logró que una abogada pro bono la acompañara. Antes de salir a la verificación, Liz habló con familiares sobre la posibilidad de que no regresara. Dice que su hija de 15 años lloraba al verla salir por la puerta.</p><p>Pero esa vez la cita salió bien.</p><p>Un fallo técnico había provocado que su monitor dejara de enviar datos de ubicación a ICE, lo que activó la verificación urgente para comprobar que no lo había cortado. Los funcionarios ajustaron el dispositivo y le dijeron que debe llevarlo durante año y medio de cumplimiento total antes de que puedan cambiarla a una aplicación para registrarse por teléfono.</p><p>"Creo que el miedo también es a que si no haces todo perfectamente, incluso con todas estas barreras, algo te va a pasar", dice Gabriela Nicolau, la abogada pro bono que acompañó a Liz.</p><p>Afuera del edificio federal, Liz dice que se sintió aliviada, por el momento. Tal vez esa vez tuvo suerte o llevar a una abogada hizo la diferencia.</p><p>Pero ese alivio es temporal. El rastreador —y la ansiedad y el miedo que conlleva— no va a desaparecer.</p><p><i>Colaboró: Keenan Chen </i></p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Chicago’s Creative Arts Workers Subsidize the Very Economic Benefits Their Crafts Accrue
entries.summary: <p>A new study shows local creatives — artists, musicians, performers and such — earn less than Illinois’ living wage.</p><p>That means they effectively subsidize their professions’ economic contributions to the city and state’s world-renowned tourism, hospitality and urban-living benefits.</p><p>The economic impact study by Arts Alliance Illinois, a statewide advocacy organization, showed musicians earning average yearly wages of $40,587; visual arts and crafts workers, $37,482; and independent creators and performers $43,832, compared with the statewide average of $50.796.</p><p>In Chicago, creators did better, but not by much. Musicians’ average yearly wage totaled $55,179; independent creators and performers $75,282, and visual arts and crafts support workers $50,519, compared with the city’s living wage of $53,667.</p><p>Solutions would require politicians, community leaders and other influencers to get creative themselves. Yet policy strategists say somehow solving one particularly bureaucratic nightmare would help tackle creatives’ plight.</p><p>It involves a little-known Chicago business license — the PPA, or Public Place of Amusement. The city requires that businesses and nonprofits obtain a Public Place of Amusement (PPA) license to host musicians, offer entertainment, or for fun activities such as bowling, karaoke and ping pong.</p><p>It’s not a new requirement. General amusement licensing has been a part of Chicago’s municipal code for more than a century.</p><p>A business seeking the PPA license that’s within 125 feet of a single-family residential zone must apply for a zoning variation — a time-consuming and intricate process that often requires the business hire lawyers.</p><p>Beth Kregor, director of the Institute for Justice Clinic (IJ Clinic) on Entrepreneurship at the University of Chicago Law School, said the clinic’s analysis shows how the PPA licenses are widely skewed in favor of neighborhoods north of Roosevelt Road (1200 South) and are concentrated in just five of the city’s 77 community areas. So creatives have few places to perform and earn money throughout the city.</p><p>The neighborhoods with no PPA licenses reflect areas where, as Kregor put it, “the businesses might have less money, fewer connections and less access to lawyers to get through this process. With less legal acumen, the complex licensing scheme will be a higher hurdle for them.”</p><p></p><p>The statistics may also challenge assumptions that entertainment venues necessarily create dangerous or illegal behavior in certain neighborhoods.</p><p>What can be done?</p><p>Advocates for PPA say businesses could help build opportunities for creatives if the city’s licensing process was less costly and complex.</p><p>Greg Fischer, owner of Chicago’s first winery, Wild Blossom Meadery & Winery, need only explain his seven-year ordeal seeking a PPA license to illustrate the obstacles he has had to overcome.</p><p>Fischer is finally near the finish line of the PPA license process.</p><p>He said the license will ensure his 10-person workforce continued employment, give wine enthusiasts the opportunity to tour the operations, and offer the community a gathering place for live entertainment ranging from standup comedians to acoustic jazz musicians.</p><p>Fischer started the winery in his South Side Beverly home garage 26 years ago. It’s unique in that he owns beekeeping operations and uses the honey to make mead that can range from sparkling to dry and crisp.</p><p>Fischer moved and expanded the winery 10 years ago by gutting and wholesale renovating a vacant 1957 construction-company building in the Washington Heights neighborhood at 91st and Hermitage. It includes classrooms, a tasting room and a backyard patio. The site backs up to the eastern edge of the Dan Ryan Woods, is a stop on the Marshall “Major” Taylor bike trail, and is 500 feet from Metra’s 91st/Beverly Hills train stop.</p><p></p><p>One homeowner who lives nearby repeatedly made baseless complaints — primarily claiming that people would sit outside in their cars drinking malt liquor — to try to stall Fischer’s plans. Fischer had to address her objections every step of the way, despite having the endorsement of then-Mayor Rahm Emanuel, former State Sen. Howard Brookins and consecutive aldermen in the ward.</p><p>“We’re like a Napa Valley winery,” Fischer said. “It’s tasting [events], not crazy parties.”</p><p>Fischer also had to twice rezone the property and remove and remediate soil toxins and underground gas tanks left from the construction company’s operations.</p><p>He said he was struck by the contrast between Chicago’s business policies and those of West Palm Beach, Florida, where he migrates the bees each year. West Palm Beach offers small businesses free setup, free mentoring, no state income tax and other incentives.</p><p>Though Fischer decided to stay in Chicago, he said, “How could any legitimate small business sustain itself [here]?”</p><p></p><p>Wineries, breweries and distilleries started efforts this spring to simplify the process.</p><p></p><p>Kregor said, “Businesses can be places where neighbors come together to experience the arts, to relax, and to have fun.</p><p></p><p>“Chicago’s current laws make it way too difficult for businesses to play that role in our neighborhoods,” she said. “By freeing more businesses to offer entertainment without a special license and simplifying the process for businesses that do need a license, City Hall can build up our creative economy, our community connections, and our reputation as an arts destination.”</p>
entries.author: Sandra Guy

entries.title: Was Bulls exec Bryson Graham actually playing 'dawg' catcher in June?
entries.summary: <p>There are still two words that grind on the teeth of most Bulls fans: Cash considerations.</p><p>A trade asset the franchise has used far too often in the last 15 years, seemingly taking the money grab over an able body to help the product on the floor. Loading the books rather than furthering the roster.</p><p>So when new executive vice president of basketball operations Bryson Graham traded his second round picks in the 2026 draft for future selections and cash considerations it felt like new GM, same as the old.</p><p>Pump the brakes on that assertion.</p><p>What if Graham was actually playing chess and not checkers, having his eyes on two players he knew he could get in free agency post-draft to ink two-way deals and keep the roster fluid?</p><p>That’s where Jaylin Sellers and Tobe Awaka come in.</p><p>They might not have the immediate talent to be every night rotation guys, but they have the makeup. “Dawgs” as some in the organization have described. And by the second half of the season, “dawgs” that could be let off the leash.</p><p>In some ways Sellers already has, playing significant minutes in Monday’s win over the Cavaliers, guarding the likes of James Harden and scoring nine points with a plus-14 in plus/minus.</p><p>“He’s a two-way player, can guard James Harden, explosive to the rim, can shoot the three,” coach Tiago Splitter described of Sellers. “He’s part of our future; we love him. He’s still developing. Got things he has to get better at but obviously had a good night.”</p><p>Sellers and Awaka were both back with the Windy City Bulls on Wednesday, while the Bulls were battling the Hornets in their final pool play game of the NBA Cup.</p><p>Expect that back and forth to continue for the time being, according to Splitter. Awaka has already shown to be a monster on the offensive boards and put that on display in late summer. As far as Sellers, the Bulls see him as a combo guard and want to make sure that he can continue working on his craft on both levels – the NBA and G League.</p><p>What Sellers doesn’t need a ton of work on? His defensive mentality. One of the reasons Splitter really likes the Providence product.</p><p>“He’s a guy who has quick feet, can create his shot,” Splitter continued. “You can see in his first possession (on the court Monday) fighting over a screen, guarding Harden. He contested a shot and then sprinted full court, this spark of energy to the group. He’s one of those guys, with ‘Ice’ (Isaac Okoro), who takes pride in defense every time. Great defender who guards his matchup with incredible energy.”</p><p>Just what this roster needs and doesn’t have enough of.</p><p>There’s a make-up to Sellers that will have staying power if the Bulls do want to be aggressive at the trade deadline. They definitely have the players to make deals come February, made easier if Sellers and Awaka continue developing – wherever they are playing.</p><p>As far as Sellers was concerned, just tell him where and when, and roll the ball out.</p><p>“If they need me, I’m here,” Sellers said of his mindset. “That’s what they keep telling me, go down there to Windy City and don’t look at it like you are just going there to be a G League killer. I want to go down there and develop. That’s what I am doing so when I come here, I can make the right reads. I feel I can fit in anywhere. If you need me to shoot the ball, I’ll shoot the ball. You need me to guard somebody, I’ll guard somebody. I’m a jack of all trades. Anything the guys need me to do, I’ll do it even if it’s bringing water. I'm like a dog in a cage. Any time they want to let me out, I'm there.”</p>
