entries.title: Obamas, spending Thanksgiving in Chicago, help pack produce at Southwest Side nonprofit
entries.summary: <p>Former President Barack Obama and First Lady Michelle Obama on Wednesday surprised employees at a Chicago Lawn nonprofit and helped pack fresh produce boxes for Chicago families in time for Thanksgiving.</p><p>A spokesperson for the Obama Foundation also confirmed the Obamas will be spending Thanksgiving in Chicago.</p><p>The Obamas arrived at Dion’s Chicago Dream around 11:50 a.m. and spent 25 minutes chatting with employees and the nonprofit’s CEO, Dion Dawson, an Englewood native and Navy veteran.</p><p>“Hello, everybody! It is good to see all of you. And all I'm saying is put us to work,” Barack Obama said. “I just want to thank Dion and Dion’s Chicago Dream. Such a wonderful concept to put fresh food together. Obviously, this is something that's been near and dear to Michelle's heart. Trying to fill these food deserts. Trying to make sure folks are getting good nutrition. And the fact that it's wonderful that so many food banks around the city have volunteers, but to be able to tie it to employment, giving people an opportunity to earn a living wage.”</p><p>Both Obamas took turns filling cardboard boxes full of fruit and veggies. As Barack Obama held a box of peppers, he joked, “In my house, I’m the brunt of all jokes. They talk about my ears. They talk about how I chew.”</p><p>“It’s loud,” Michelle Obama said. “It’s loud.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-050000" name="image-050000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8d784ae/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F31%2F22%2F0103a6e04393adf59f07001a08c6%2Fobamas-261126-17.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3f42bb0/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F31%2F22%2F0103a6e04393adf59f07001a08c6%2Fobamas-261126-17.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0f84177/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F31%2F22%2F0103a6e04393adf59f07001a08c6%2Fobamas-261126-17.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Michelle and Barack Obama help pack produce at a Southwest Side nonprofit Wednesday. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0f84177/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F31%2F22%2F0103a6e04393adf59f07001a08c6%2Fobamas-261126-17.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e05cbda/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F31%2F22%2F0103a6e04393adf59f07001a08c6%2Fobamas-261126-17.JPG 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0f84177/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F31%2F22%2F0103a6e04393adf59f07001a08c6%2Fobamas-261126-17.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Michelle and Barack Obama help pack produce at a Southwest Side nonprofit Wednesday.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The former president laughed it off and told the employees, “You all stop laughing.”</p><p>Dawson asked both Obamas to list one thing they learned about themselves within the last year.</p><p>“I learned I’m getting older. It’s a shock that I’m getting older,” President Obama said. He also joked that “it used to be that the only time you got hurt was when you fell or something.”</p><p>“Now you just make a move and say “Ah, what was that?’" Barack Obama said.</p><p>Michelle Obama said: “With age comes deep wisdom.”</p><p>Both Obamas helped to pack the boxes before loading them into a freezer. The produce that arrives at the center is delivered within 24 hours, just in time for Thanksgiving. Dawson said his company purchases, packs and delivers and to date, has delivered more than nine million pounds of fresh produce.</p><p>The Obamas took a photo with employees and left around 12:15 p.m.</p><p>Dawson later told the pool his nonprofit delivers to 5,400 households a week, and 180 ZIP codes in all 77 Chicago neighborhoods.</p><p>Dawson said the visit was a complete surprise and he was told about it about an hour before they arrived.</p><p>“We met two of the most iconic people on the planet, and it was crazy. It was amazing. But I mean, all in all, I'm really excited for my team,” Dawson said. “I think that the dopest thing is my team being able to be recognized for their work, but also people see it in action. So being able to have the president and First Lady see the quality that we have to build boxes with us. Even the people receiving this week, they won't even know that some of their boxes were made by the president, First Lady. So it’s just amazing.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-5d0000" name="image-5d0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/150f868/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F72%2Ff6%2F6e62b6e64ef59d9149d898e6efa4%2Fobamas-261126-22.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9c3ce54/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F72%2Ff6%2F6e62b6e64ef59d9149d898e6efa4%2Fobamas-261126-22.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/feb5b9f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F72%2Ff6%2F6e62b6e64ef59d9149d898e6efa4%2Fobamas-261126-22.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Barack and Michelle Obama help pack produce at a Southwest Side nonprofit Wednesday. entries.title: Two people arrested during Midway Blitz sue federal government
entries.summary: <p>A man and a woman who detailed traumatic experiences while being arrested during Operation Midway Blitz have filed separate lawsuits against the federal government. </p><p>Dayanne Figueroa and Luis Jesus Acosta Gutierrez each filed lawsuits Monday in the Northern District of Illinois seeking compensation and accountability for the actions of the federal agents involved in their arrests. </p><p>Acosta Gutierrez was driving to a mechanic to get his car fixed in Elgin on the morning of Dec. 6 when an unmarked vehicle carrying federal agents cut in front of him before striking his car from the passenger side. </p><p>"The car came very close to mine and hit me from behind. My car spun around, made a 360-degree turn. I was looking right at them, face to face. I grabbed my phone and my wallet and ran," Acosta Gutierrez told a Sun-Times reporter in Spanish. "I had never seen anything like that in my life. I wasn’t going to be arrested; I hadn’t done anything."</p><p>Acosta Gutierrez said the agents yelled "Stop, cabrón! Stop! It’ll be worse!”</p><p>"The whole process felt like psychological and mental torture," Acosta Gutierrez said. </p><p>While running, he came across a man taking out the trash and told him to flee due to the presence of agents. </p><p>The two fled into the man's home in the 1600 block of Maple Lane, where Acosta Gutierrez stayed barricaded for hours as crowds of nearby residents, protesters and rapid responders formed. </p><p>Acosta Gutierrez, who came to the United States from Venezuela in 2023 to work and create a better life for himself and for his family, tried showing agents his work permit and Social Security card, to no avail. </p><p>Eventually, agents got to Acosta Gutierrez and struck him in the face <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/12/09/dhs-arrest-elgin-tren-de-aragua-immigration" >as they detained him</a>, he said. </p><p>"I started asking them to forgive me for the trouble," Acosta Gutierrez said. "They grabbed me with long guns pointed at me and made me feel like a criminal."</p><p>After his arrest, Acosta Gutierrez spent several weeks at Miami Correctional Facility in Indiana before being taken briefly to Louisiana. From there, the government flew him to Venezuela. His departure was legally classified as voluntary, according to his attorney, Robert Held.</p><p></p><p>The Department of Homeland Security have previously called Acosta Gutierrez a suspected member of the Venezuelan gang <a class="Link" href="https://www.dhs.gov/news/2025/12/08/suspected-tren-de-aragua-gang-member-released-country-biden-administration-rams-law" target="_blank" >Tren de Aragua</a> — a claim Acosta Gutierrez denies. </p><p>"I’m not the kind of person they say I am, a criminal or a gang member. This has affected my life in every way, economically and mentally," Acosta Gutierrez said. "I’m sick now. I’m not the same as before. And I want justice — not just for me, but also for people who are going through what I went through, which was unjust."</p><p>About two months earlier, on the morning of Oct. 10, Figueroa, a United States citizen, was driving to work after dropping her son off at school when federal agents in an unmarked red van trying to drive away from a hostile crowd swerved into her vehicle in the 1600 block of West Hubbard Street in West Town, according to the complaint. </p><p>Agents forcibly dragged her from her car, handcuffed her, knelt on her body near a surgical incision and detained her despite pleas that she was recovering from kidney surgery, the complaint states. </p><p>“What happened to me is what happens to people when our government is allowed to act with impunity and trample our Constitution," Figueroa said in a press release. "They have made a mockery of everything this country claims to stand for, and I hope this lawsuit helps hold those responsible for my attack accountable, and puts an end to this horrific abuse.”</p><p>Figueroa's lawsuit alleges false arrest, false imprisonment, assault, battery, negligence and the intentional infliction of emotional distress . </p><p>She was one of five U.S. citizens who spoke at a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/12/09/tammy-duckworth-senate-hearing-illegal-dhs-arrests-chicago-woman-testimony" target="_blank" >congressional public forum</a>, last December. They wanted to counter DHS claims that the department does not arrest U.S. citizens. </p><p>Figueroa also was taken to Broadview and then to a facility in Lombard. She said the blood in her urine finally prompted agents to allow her to get medical help, and she contacted her boyfriend while in an ambulance. In all, she was in custody several hours.</p><p>"Ms. Figueroa has endured one of the most horrifying experiences imaginable — having her personal safety attacked by masked ICE agents who took the law into their own hands,” said attorney Luis Carrillo.</p><p>"She is tremendously courageous for speaking out not just for herself, but for the voiceless who cannot speak. We look forward to joining the fight for justice for her."<br></p>
entries.author: Alma Campos

entries.title: Steelers QB Aaron Rodgers says teammate told him about benching
entries.summary: <p>PITTSBURGH — Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers said Wednesday he found out about his surprise benching for this week's game against Denver from a teammate and not coach Mike McCarthy.</p><p>The team announced late Tuesday that Rodgers would be inactive for Friday's game against the Broncos, with Mason Rudolph set to start — a shock announcement coming hours after McCarthy had publicly committed to Rodgers remaining the starter after an ugly offensive showing in a loss to Philadelphia.</p><p>A day later, Rodgers went on ESPN's "The Pat McAfee Show" and said he learned of his benching from tight end Pat Freiermuth, while also saying it came after he had spoken up to McCarthy about the coach falling asleep in position meetings or missing team events.</p><p>Rodgers said he had discussed McCarthy's inattentiveness with the coach and had talked to him about changing play-calling duties.</p><p>"If you try and bench me or don't change the play calling then you should just release me, because I feel like at this point, I'm doing what's right for the organization," Rodgers said.</p><p>"He responded with, I'm going to do what's right by the organization, which in his mind was getting rid of me," Rodgers added. "Now obviously he got the owner and the GM on his side."</p><p>The Steelers benching the four-time Most Valuable Player is a stunning move that leaves the soon-to-be 43-year-old's future very much in doubt.</p><p>Rodgers wasn't around to see the Steelers begin the process of moving on without him. The team, which already indicated Rodgers would be inactive against the Broncos, excused him from practice on Wednesday while Mason Rudolph took snaps with the starters.</p><p>Then he popped up as a guest on McAfee's show.</p><p>Rodgers has already said this will be his last season. Now it's fair to wonder if he'll reach the end of it — in Pittsburgh anyway — after coach Mike McCarthy turned to Rudolph, a longtime backup, with the Steelers (6-4) trying to snap out of a two-game funk before it's too late.</p><p>There's little precedent for sitting a future Hall of Famer and Super Bowl winner midseason. Johnny Unitas, playing out his final days in a Chargers uniform, got benched for rookie Dan Fouts after four games in 1973.</p><p>Joe Namath never played again after throwing four picks in a loss to the Bears during a late-career cameo for the Los Angeles Rams a month into the 1977 season.</p><p>More recently, Denver replaced Peyton Manning with Brock Osweiler midway through 2015 even with the club sitting at 7-2. Manning returned in the season finale and then served as a game manager in the playoffs as the Broncos' dominant defense led the franchise to its third Super Bowl victory.</p><p>Manning walked off the field with the Lombardi Trophy in tow in his final game.</p><p>This is not that.</p><p>While the Steelers are currently in playoff position, their next three games are against AFC West-leading Denver, surging Houston, and AFC South leader Jacksonville. While they can probably withstand one loss or maybe even two, three could be catastrophic.</p><p>Enter Rudolph, who rescued Pittsburgh's season and briefly earned folk hero status in 2023 by coming off the bench in December and authoring a surge to a playoff berth.</p><p>That didn't stop the Steelers from moving on from him immediately, bringing in Russell Wilson and Justin Fields in 2024 and then Rodgers in 2025, a move designed to help Pittsburgh end a postseason victory drought that's nearing a decade.</p><p>Rodgers' first year ended with a blowout playoff loss at home to the Texans. His future seemed uncertain until the Steelers hired Mike McCarthy to replace Mike Tomlin in January, a job Rodgers played a hand in helping McCarthy land, though how big a hand is up for debate.</p><p>Not that it mattered in the end. Rodgers opted to make one last run at a championship while reuniting with the coach he won a Super Bowl with in early 2011.</p><p>A storybook ending on the field seems remote. Pittsburgh is a woeful 2-4 on the road, where it figures to be when the playoffs start if the Steelers can't track down Cincinnati in the race for the AFC North title.</p><p>And the team's Jekyll/Hyde play in general has offered little tangible proof that it is a legitimate threat to have an extended postseason stay.</p><p>Rodgers' play has mirrored that of his team. He tossed three touchdowns in three consecutive weeks, even outdueling Cincinnati star Joe Burrow in a victory over the Bengals in late September.</p><p>Yet he's struggled to make an impact of late, often checking the ball down to running backs Jaylen Warren and Rico Dowdle or taking sacks behind an inconsistent offensive line when trying to push the ball down the field to a receiving group that has underperformed, particularly two-time Pro Bowler DK Metcalf.</p><p>Rodgers averaged just 0.5 air yards per attempt in the first half last week against Philadelphia, the lowest since ESPN began measuring the stat in 2006.</p><p>What happens next to a player who has always leaned into doing things on his terms at all times is unclear. He has leaned into being a Steeler at his third and supposedly last NFL stop.</p><p>It was that way on Tuesday afternoon, when Rodgers traded jokes with Rudolph and longtime defensive tackle Cam Heyward after addressing reporters.</p><p>Barely eight hours later, he was no longer the starter. There's a chance sometime soon he might not even be a Steeler, the latest and perhaps final twist in a journey that will end with him getting a gold jacket at the Pro Football Hall of Fame, even if this ends up being an inglorious off-ramp for all involved.<br></p>

entries.title: Bears Jeffery Simmons' arrival has unlocked the best of longtime friend Montez Sweat
entries.summary: <p>As <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> defensive end Montez Sweat laughed on the sideline while celebrating the first safety of his career <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/22/bears-dt-jeffery-simmons-embraces-the-moment-with-3-sacks-in-a-21-13-win-over-saints" >Sunday against the Saints</a>, a giant of a man grabbed him by the back of the collar and yelled something that made him laugh even harder.</p><p>That man was new defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons, and he’s one of the few who could whirl his 6-foot-6, 270-pound teammate around like that. He’s also a rare individual who can say just about whatever he wants to Sweat, and that’s exactly the presence Sweat needed.</p><p>After two sacks in his first five games this season, Sweat has matched that in three games playing with Simmons. They go into the Bears’ game Thursday at the Lions with a combined seven in their last three games, swinging the team’s biggest concern into one of its strengths.</p><p>Simmons instantly became a captain-type figure when he arrived at Halas Hall late last month. Not only is he excellent on the field, but he spoke in detail about the effort he has put into learning how to reach all different types of teammates, though he veered from that when mentioning Sweat.</p><p>“He’s been around me long enough,” Simmons said. “I could go talk to him a little crazy.”</p><p>He’s been lighting a fire under Sweat ever since.</p><p>The two describe their relationship as brotherly, tracing it back to playing on the defensive line together at Mississippi State, but it’s unmistakably clear that Simmons is the big brother.</p><p>As accomplished as Sweat is, he’s been averse to taking on that kind of role since the Bears acquired him in 2023. He’s relatively quiet and hasn’t ever seemed comfortable stepping forward as one of the key voices of the defense. He needed Simmons.</p><p>Simmons is in his ear almost constantly. They line up next to each other on the field in practice and games, they usually sit near each other on the bench and they’re next-door neighbors in the locker room.</p><p>Simmons’ message mostly seems to be, from his telling of it, shut up and play better.</p><p>“I’m challenging the heck out of him,” he said, adding that Sweat pushes him as well.</p><p>Simmons always tells Sweat, “Need more, need more,” which couldn’t be more fitting for Sweat and the Bears. He’s been good, but this team has needed him to be great. And Sweat has responded to it, calling his effect “a great boost” and having him around “a good feeling.”</p><p>When Simmons grabbed him by the collar, he couldn’t have been prouder. Earlier in the game, Sweat had come to him on the sideline complaining about something the Saints had done to thwart him, and Simmons wasn’t hearing it. He turned to Sweat and said only, “OK,” then told him how to beat it the next time and moved on.</p><p>No excuses. Just results.</p><p>“I know when he’s kind of in his head,” Simmons said. “For me, it’s, ‘Be in this moment. Let it come to you.’</p><p>“It’s amazing that when he just gets in his bag and is himself, [the safety] happened. That’s why I’m excited to be here: I know he’s got so much more in the tank. It’s just beginning.”</p><p>Part of how the Bears justified giving up two first-round picks in the trade was their belief that Simmons would have a ripple effect. Not only is he a star, but he has the ability to enhance the pieces they already had. Nowhere is that more evident than with Sweat.</p>

entries.title: Bears rule out CB Kyler Gordon vs. Lions, marking 2nd consecutive missed game
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> nickel cornerback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/13/bears-cb-kyler-gordon-is-back-from-the-depths-of-injuries-i-still-havent-shown-my-true-potential" >Kyler Gordon</a> will miss his second consecutive game after the team ruled him out for Thursday against the Lions.</p><p>Gordon injured his left shoulder against the Buccaneers on Nov. 8 and hasn't played or practiced since. He came back in after coming out of that game and getting checked by the training staff.</p><p>Injuries are a sensitive subject when it comes to Gordon, who missed 14 regular-season games last season and was out most of the offseason before missing the first five games this season.</p><p>Throughout his absence, Bears general manager Ryan Poles and coach Ben Johnson expressed frustration, and Poles indicated there had been a disconnect between Gordon and the team on his recovery.</p><p>Gordon has 13 tackles, including four sacks, in four games.</p><p>The Bears also ruled out running back Roschon Johnson (ankle) and safety Elijah Hicks (concussion).</p><p>Cornerback Tyrique Stevenson was added to the injury report Wednesday with a groin issue and is listed as questionable. Linebacker D'Marco Jackson (elbow), is questionable as well.</p><p>The team elevated running back Salvon Ahmed and defensive back Elijah Jones from the practice squad for Thursday.</p>

entries.title: Andy Taylor, guitarist of new wave icons Duran Duran, dies at 65
entries.summary: <p>Andy Taylor, the original guitarist of the 1980s English new wave <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/hub/music" target="_blank" >band Duran Duran,</a> whose huge pop hits included “Hungry Like the Wolf,” “The Reflex” and “Rio” and were inextricably linked to the launch of MTV, has died. He was 65.</p><p>Taylor's death was confirmed by his family and band mates in a statement posted on social media and Duran Duran's website.</p><p>“From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music. His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed,” the band said.</p><p>On the night he was inducted in the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in November 2022, Taylor revealed that he had been battling stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer for several years and was unable to attend.</p><p>“I would like to thank each of my brothers in this great band,” he wrote. “You can dream about what happened to us but to experience it, on one’s own terms, as mates, was beyond incredible.”</p><p>The two-time Grammy Award-winners had nine gold records and six platinum ones, with 20 Top 20 singles in the UK and 18 in the U.S. They were two-time Ivor Novello Award winners and are MTV Video Visionary Award recipients.</p><p>The band’s 1981 debut album “Duran Duran” had their first hit single, “Planet Earth,” but it was “Rio” that transformed them into trans-Atlantic stars. The Rock Hall explained their appeal this way: “They were new wave outsiders who became music video stars — “Tiger Beat” fashion pinups who rocked arenas.”</p><div class="Enhancement" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor listens as a fellow band member answers a question at a news conference in Hong Kong in 2004.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>AP Photo/Lo Sai-hung</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>How music videos made Duran Duran massively famous</h3><p>The band’s imperial stage occurred with a trio of hit albums between 1981 and 1983, with such dance-floor barnburners as “Girls on Film” and “Union of the Snake” and the moody ballads “The Chauffeur” and “Save a Prayer.” Other hits in the coming years included “The Wild Boys,” “New Moon on Monday” and “Come Undone.” Their popularity was cemented when they recorded the James Bond theme song “A View to a Kill” and earned a slot at Live Aid in 1985.</p><p>Mixing fashion, pioneering synthesizers and glam-pop swagger, the telegenic band were all over radio and young people’s walls, with bassist John Taylor and singer Simon Le Bon becoming heartthrobs and the band being labeled part of the New Romantics. Princess Diana was known to be a fan and that meant a lot to the band.</p><p>“It worked well for us,” drummer Roger Taylor told Rolling Stone. “It was genuine. I don’t think it was some sort of PR stunt. It was massive for us because she was the No. 1 icon of the early ’80s.”</p><p>The band’s success was in large part due to their videos, including their Antigua-set song “Rio,” which featured shots of the band in pastel suits sailing confidently on a yacht. For the album “Rio,” they shot three music videos in Sri Lanka — including “Save a Prayer,” which had John Taylor getting sprayed by an elephant — and two in Antigua, feeding MTV’s need to have a stream of visuals, something classic rock didn’t have.</p><p>“A lot of the success of the album is down to the power of the videos and the way it made the band omnipresent around the globe,” Le Bon told The Daily Beast in 2012. Andy Taylor agreed: “I don’t think we could have done it without MTV.”</p><p>John Taylor and keyboardist Nick Rhodes started the band as teenagers in the northern city of Birmingham in 1978, with a name inspired by a character in the Jane Fonda-starring sci-fi movie “Barbarella.” Roger Taylor, Le Bon and Andy Taylor joined soon after, with the British press referring to them as the “Fab Five.” Andy Taylor answered an ad in Melody Maker music magazine for a “Live-Wire Guitarist.” (None of the Taylors were related.)</p><p>“We all grew up on the same vinyl records and live gigs, from David Bowie to Roxy Music, The Sex Pistols and, of course, Chic. I could go to all those places as a player and developed a hybrid guitar style that fitted this amazing concept of a band,” Andy Taylor wrote in a letter read by the band during their Rock Hall induction.</p><h3>Behind massive success, Taylor and band mates were distant</h3><p>Duran Duran had the unenviable job of following Led Zeppelin at Live Aid in Philadelphia and performed “A View to a Kill,” “The Union of the Snake,” “Save a Prayer” and “The Reflex.” In his book, “Wild Child,” Andy Taylor revealed the band was, as he put it, “falling apart at the seams.”</p><p>“Everything should have been perfect, but privately we were screwed and in turmoil. When we came offstage in Philadelphia there were no congratulatory hugs or friendly smiles. It was like we were completely foreign to each other, and it would be the last time we played together for almost two decades.”</p><p>The various members all had some success with side projects: Le Bon, Rhodes and Roger Taylor recorded an album as Arcadia in 1985; John Taylor and Andy Taylor formed Power Station, a supergroup that included Robert Palmer, in 1984, having hits with “Some Like It Hot” and “Get It On.”</p><p>In 1986, the band came together to record the hit album produced with Nile Rodgers “Notorious” — with hits including the title single and “Skin Trade” — but Andy Taylor made his second exit from the group after some early recording sessions for the album. He would stay away for such albums as 1997's “Medazzaland” and 2000′s “Pop Trash” — but returned for 2004's “Astronaut.”</p><p>By 2007, Andy Taylor opted not to participate in the Timbaland-led “Red Carpet Massacre,” an attempt to harness a more youthful rhythmic vibe. “With Andy not turning up, it couldn’t be a rock record, so that whole album was an attempt to patch over the cracks with Andy missing,” John Taylor told The Atlanta Journal-Constitution in 2011.</p><p>Andy Taylor told The Scotsman in 2008: “People have wrongly assumed that I didn’t want to be in the band, but the opposite is true. I always wanted to be in a band, but Duran Duran had ceased to function as a band.”</p><p>At Duran Duran’s height, they were as famously destructive as any rock band. Andy Taylor in his memoir revealed he had a six-year cocaine habit and band members trashed hotel rooms, argued with management about money and had high-end shopping sprees.</p><p>Andy Taylor was the first of the Duran boys to get married, tying the knot with Tracey in 1982 and having four children, Andy, Georgie, Bethy and Izzy, and a grandson, Albie. He is survived by all of them, and they credited his devotion to them in a family statement.</p><p>“For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first. Nothing made him happier than having us all together, and no matter how far music took him, his heart was always at home,” the family statement said.</p><p>In 2023, he released the album “Man’s a Wolf to Man,” his first solo release in over 30 years. On the title track, he sang: “Last night/I dreamt someone loved me/And life was not surreal/Someone’s souvenir.”</p>

entries.title: Pat McAfee didn't need to be an interviewer to let Aaron Rodgers sound off on Mike McCarthy
entries.summary: <p>There isn’t an NFL insider in the world who could’ve provided the information that quarterback Aaron Rodgers revealed Wednesday.</p><p>And there isn’t a show where that could’ve happened other than “The Pat McAfee Show.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/nfl/2026/11/25/aaron-rodgers-pat-mcafee-steelers-benching" >Rodgers’ time with the Steelers,</a> and perhaps in the NFL, ended after he shared intimate details of coach Mike McCarthy’s behavior behind the scenes, including falling asleep in meetings and breaking halftime Sunday by saying, “One, two, three, Packers!”</p><p>McCarthy was Rodgers’ coach with the Packers from 2006 to ’18.</p><p>Late Tuesday, the Steelers announced that Rodgers, who has started all season, would be inactive for the game Friday against the Broncos. Midday Wednesday, Rodgers went on McAfee’s show, which he used to do weekly for $1 million a year, to explain what happened — and it was jaw-dropping.</p><p>Rodgers said tight end Pete Freiermuth was the one who told him he’d be inactive, not McCarthy. Rodgers said McCarthy snored during meetings and missed others. And he said that behavior went all the way back to McCarthy’s time in Green Bay.</p><p>“It began as concern for him,” Rodgers said of his recent intervention with McCarthy. “ ‘We’ve been together a long time. I want the best for you, but you’re starting to lose the team.’ ”</p><p>McCarthy calls the plays, and Rodgers thought that duty should belong to someone else. He said he was “doing what’s right for the organization.”</p><p>“I’m not saying it to [expletive] bury you,” Rodgers said. “I’m saying that because these habits are not healthy and they’re not becoming of someone calling the plays.”</p><p>Rodgers said McCarthy denied falling asleep, but Rodgers said “everybody knows the truth,” even mentioning that players would text each other on the team bus about it. He said the last straw was McCarthy saying “One, two, three, Packers!” in the Steelers’ locker room.</p><p>The revelations were such that McAfee looked like he was going to keel over, saying he was “flabbergasted.” McAfee isn’t a trained interviewer, and he essentially said as much. The only hint of pushback was McAfee emphasizing that Rodgers was giving his side of the story.</p><p>But McAfee isn’t looking to be a journalist. He’s looking to get attention-grabbing guests, and there are few bigger than Rodgers. That’s why McAfee’s deal with ESPN is valued at $30 million a year and why he has become a centerpiece among the network’s talent.</p><p>Despite his lack of training, McAfee was smart enough to just let Rodgers talk. Rodgers was so measured in his tone that he was completely believable, and he said his teammates could back up each of his claims.</p><p>“If you're standing on the truth and the facts … it’s not opinion that I’m sharing; it’s facts,” Rodgers said, which is rich considering what he spewed when COVID was one of his favorite topics. “I mean, it’s firsthand facts.”</p><p>Co-host A.J. Hawk, who was with McCarthy and Rodgers in Green Bay, seemingly confirmed everything Rodgers was saying by, well, saying nothing, though he did ask two questions during the 36-minute segment.</p><p>Rodgers said the situation extends to how McCarthy’s time with the Packers ended.</p><p>“In Mike’s mind, I got him fired in 2018,” Rodgers said. “He told a staff member that.”</p><p>McAfee was careful to consider McCarthy’s situation, saying he was concerned for his health. McCarthy appeared on the show between coaching jobs — he also coached the Cowboys from 2020 to ’24 before joining the Steelers this season. The team said it’s sticking with McCarthy as it holds the seventh and final AFC playoff seed at 6-4 with Mason Rudolph now at quarterback.</p><p>Rodgers has said this will be the last of his 22 NFL seasons, but he never foresaw it ending like this. After being waived, Rodgers could catch on with one of several teams in need of a quarterback, including the rival Ravens. Or he could make his last day in the NFL memorable for what he said, not how he played.</p><p>And he can thank McAfee for that.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/nfl/2026/11/25/aaron-rodgers-pat-mcafee-steelers-benching" >Steelers cut Aaron Rodgers after QB criticized coach Mike McCarthy on ‘The Pat McAfee Show’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: New FAA rules could affect takeoffs at O'Hare and Midway ahead of busy Thanksgiving travel weekend
entries.summary: <p>The Federal Aviation Administration introduced new requirements for air traffic controllers Tuesday that could change how departing planes are cleared for takeoff, just as Chicago airports prepare for a record-breaking Thanksgiving travel week.</p><p>The new rules apply nationwide, including at O'Hare and Midway, and require additional staffing and supervision when controllers use a procedure called "line up and wait."</p><p>The procedure allows a departing plane to enter a runway and wait there for takeoff clearance, rather than remaining on a taxiway until the runway is clear. It helps airports move departing planes more quickly during busy periods.</p><p>Under the new rules, the controller directing arriving and departing planes cannot simultaneously handle another control position. A dedicated supervisor must also oversee the operation without taking on other duties.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure controllers have adequate supervision. The agency said the new requirements "will not impact airport operations."</p><p>The policy comes as Chicago's airports prepare for more than two million travelers during the Thanksgiving period, according to airline projections cited by the Chicago Department of Aviation.</p><p>Nearly 1.67 million travelers are expected at O'Hare between Tuesday and Monday, a 7.2% increase from last year and a Thanksgiving travel week record for the airport. Midway is projected to see more than 353,000 passengers, nearly 2% more than in 2025.</p><p>The changes occur less than two weeks after a nationwide ground stop disrupted thousands of flights. Separately, O'Hare experienced a ground stop Monday attributed to staffing constraints at Chicago's air traffic control facilities.</p><p>The Chicago Department of Aviation did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the policy's potential implications for O'Hare and Midway.</p>

entries.title: Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade postponed to Saturday due to expected bad weather
entries.summary: <p>Macy’s 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed from Thursday to Saturday as powerful winds are expected to bear down on New York during the annual event, organizers said Wednesday.</p><p>In a statement, NBC cited conversations with the city and concerns over the safety of participants and spectators due to expected “extreme weather.” A rerun of the 2025 parade will air Thursday and the parade will now kick off at 8:30 a.m. Saturday, Macy’s said in a statement.</p><p>“Our team is now working through the complex operational logistics required to bring the Parade to life on Saturday, and we will share additional details as they are finalized,” Macy’s said. “We are incredibly grateful to the thousands of volunteers, performers and partners who make this extraordinary tradition possible. We can’t wait to celebrate 100 years of Parade magic together on Saturday.”</p><p>A representative for the Marching Illini confirmed to the Sun-Times that the band had also been informed of the postponement by Macy’s and NBC, and that it was actively trying to make contingency plans to attempt to make the performance happen Saturday morning.</p><p>The group, made up of 410 members, is one of 10 marching bands that had been selected for this year’s rendition of the century-old, annual holiday tradition. It would have been its second time performing in the parade, the first coming in 2015.</p><p>The band had boarded buses to New York City Sunday after performing at the final Illini home football game of the year Saturday, the band previously said in a <a class="Link" href="https://news.illinois.edu/marching-illini-prepare-for-performance-at-100th-macys-thanksgiving-day-parade/" target="_blank" ><u>statement</u></a>. In total, the $600,000 trip came with a cost of $275 for each student, while the rest of the trip was covered by donations and grants; two more days would come with rearranging transportation and more hotel costs.</p><p></p><p></p><p>New York City is expected to get blasted with wind gusts between 50 to 60 mph on Thursday, along with steady, sustained winds between 30 to 38 mph, according to city emergency management officials. Moderate to heavy rain is also expected.</p><p>Separately, the National Weather Service has issued a high wind warning and a coastal flood warning for Thursday into Friday.</p><p>The parade’s iconic balloons were well on the way to being inflated when the postponement was announced. Macy’s representatives had repeatedly put off interviews with media on-site.</p><p>The city <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/macys-thanksgiving-parade-new-york-weather-storm-3a0da094f00b04a073b33ffb2c03d040" target="_blank" ><u>has long had</u></a> measures in place that dictate whether to lower the balloons or cancel their flights entirely if the wind gets too strong, due to concerns that strong winds can knock them off course and into spectators along the parade route.</p><p>The city’s balloon rules were put in place after high winds sent a Cat in the Hat balloon careening into a metal pole during the 1997 parade, leaving a woman in a coma.</p><p>Bad weather in the past has caused balloons to be flown a bit lower than usual, with each inflatable character having a distinct risk profile that includes its size and weight and optimal altitudes for differing wind speeds.</p>

entries.title: Chicago could lose federal funding if it doesn’t get the lead pipes out faster
entries.summary: <p>It’s been five years since Congress passed a landmark $15 billion bill to replace toxic lead service lines nationwide. But the effort is approaching a "funding cliff" — and Chicago is falling dangerously behind, according to a report Wednesday from the U.S. Sen. Tammy Duckworth.</p><p>The city has replaced just 4% of its more than 400,000 lead service lines, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/06/30/chicago-has-most-lead-pipes-why-is-it-so-expensive-to-replace-them" target="_blank" >most of any U.S. city, </a>according to Duckworth’s report. Meanwhile, federal funding that’s helped pay for the work is running out, with no clear path to replace it.</p><p>The $15 billion approved under the 2021 bipartisan infrastructure law is expiring while the Trump administration has proposed cutting drinking water revolving fund assistance by 90%. Congress also reduced the program by <a class="Link" href="https://grist.org/politics/states-say-they-need-more-help-replacing-lead-pipes-congress-may-cut-the-funding-instead/" target="_blank" >an additional $125 million.</a></p><p>The expiration date comes as the Environmental Protection Agency’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.epa.gov/newsreleases/biden-harris-administration-issues-final-rule-requiring-replacement-lead-pipes-within" target="_blank" >10-year deadline</a> for removing the nation’s lead pipes is now taking effect, requiring most water systems to complete replacements by 2037. Chicago has until 2047 due to its large number of lead lines, said Erik Olson, senior director of health at the Natural Resources Defense Council. </p><h3>Chicago remains behind replacing lead pipes</h3><p>As of this month, the city's Department of Public Health said it's replaced 18,000 lead service lines. But at its current pace, Olson said the city faces a steep challenge in meeting even the extended deadline.</p><p>Olson has spent the last 30 years trying to get lead pipes out of cities. For him, Chicago’s slow progress reflects decades of political and institutional inaction.</p><p>“A lot of cities have been dragging their feet on this for decades — and Chicago, in particular,” Olson said. “It seems that a lot of cities just have not taken this problem seriously, until finally the EPA put its foot down."</p><p>The public health stakes are significant, as there's no safe level of lead exposure, particularly for children. Even water systems that meet EPA’s lead action level of 15 parts per billion are not necessarily safe, Olson explained.</p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2853806" target="_blank" >September 2026 study</a> found that children drinking water from lead pipes can have elevated blood lead levels even in cities such as Flint, Michigan, that fall below the EPA threshold.</p><p>“Being below EPA’s action level does not mean that the lead levels are safe for kids,” Olson said.</p><p>Lead exposure also poses serious risks to adults, he said, including pregnant women and people vulnerable to cardiovascular disease, underscoring why removing the pipes must remain a public health priority.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.duckworth.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/getting_the_lead_out_duckworth.pdf" target="_blank" >Duckworth’s report</a> details the widening gap between the nation’s replacement efforts and resources needed to finish the job. More than 4 million lead service lines remain nationwide, and the report estimates over 400,000 pipes need to be replaced annually to meet the 2037 deadline — about four times the current pace.</p><h3>Cities like Chicago must ‘up their game’ to replace pipes</h3><p>Illinois has received $1.18 billion in federal funding, more than any other state. But that money, Duckworth said, hasn't guaranteed progress.</p><p>“Money alone doesn’t remove pipes,” Duckworth said, calling for coordinated action from local, state and federal officials.</p><p>Duckworth is urging cities to adopt mandatory replacement programs and tackle the work block by block, like Newark, New Jersey, which replaced more than 23,000 lines in less than three years through an aggressive citywide program.</p><p>Olson said Newark demonstrates what political commitment can accomplish.</p><p>“Even with 20 years, they’re going to have to really pick up their game, and they have not really done that yet,” he said of Chicago. “The city with big shoulders really ought to be thinking seriously about fixing this problem.”</p><p>Olson said he hopes the EPA deadline, coupled with a new Democrat majority entering Congress, will usher in new momentum for water infrastructure in 2027.</p><p>But without faster replacements and sustained funding, Olson said the health of cities like Chicago hangs in the balance.</p><p>“It means you've at least a generation of kids that will continue to be exposed to lead,” Olson said. “You're foregoing just enormous public health benefits and other benefits because you're not replacing those lead pipes, and it's really inexcusable to be taking this long.”</p>

entries.title: Ex policía de Chicago se declara culpable de ayudar a contrabandear armas a México
entries.summary: <p>Un exagente de la Policía de Chicago se declaró culpable el lunes de haber participado en un plan para contrabandear armas a México después de usar su placa policial para comprarlas, según registros judiciales.</p><p>Kevin Rodríguez, de 28 años, se declaró culpable el lunes en la Corte de Distrito de Estados Unidos. Ahora podría enfrentar hasta unos ocho años de prisión en su audiencia de sentencia el 17 de febrero.</p><p>Rodríguez fue acusado el año pasado en una imputación federal por cargos de conspiración, un delito grave, relacionados con dos ventas de armas en 2024. Diego Valdez, también imputado, le habría indicado a Rodríguez que comprara dos armas, incluido un fusil tipo AR. Rodríguez supuestamente aceptó comprarlas utilizando sus credenciales del departamento de policía, según la acusación.</p><p>Los dos hombres viajaron a Indiana y Rodríguez compró un fusil, según la acusación. Luego, unos días después, Rodríguez compró una pistola en Monee, Illinois. Unos meses después, Valdez llevó las armas a México, dice la acusación.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-9d0000" name="module-9d0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Valdez supuestamente le pagó entonces a Rodríguez más de $2,600 mediante la aplicación de Zelle alrededor de la fecha de la compra de las armas. Valdez habría contrabandeado las armas a México con la intención de venderlas, según la acusación.</p><p>Valdez no solicitó permiso estatal para poseer un arma de asalto, dice la acusación.</p><p>El abogado de Rodríguez no respondió de inmediato a las solicitudes de comentario.</p><p>Rodríguez fue reconocido por el sindicato Fraternal Order of Police (FOP) por su papel en una persecución en auto en 2022, durante la cual quedó ensartado sobre una barda de hierro forjado y siguió persiguiendo a una persona que huyó de un auto robado hacía un complejo de apartamentos en el sur de Chicago.</p><p>Pero también fue objeto de varias quejas durante su tiempo en el departamento de policía, entre ellas no haber notificado al departamento ni presentar papeleo sobre una persecución en 2022. También se le acusó de abuso verbal y de detener a un conductor sin causa probable.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Chicago-area businesses' feelings are mixed about Small Business Saturday
entries.summary: <p>Holly House owner Samantha Frontera hopes the holiday shopping season kick-starts the registers at her Lincoln Park and Orland Park boutiques.</p><p>Sonat Birnecker Hart expects her company, Koval Distillery’s Cranberry Gin, and small-batch bourbons will be the preferred stocking stuffers.</p><p>Alizé Bikard is hopeful that consumers will flock to her new French bakery, Guillotine, in West Town.</p><p>The expectations among business owners ahead of Small Business Saturday run the gamut, as consumer concerns linger over escalating living costs and pricier goods and services.</p><p>Last year, Small Business Saturday generated an estimated $18 billion in U.S. consumer spending, according to American Express, which created the designation in 2010 to encourage consumers to shop at locally owned businesses. But the figure is about a 19% drop from 2024, when consumers reported spending $22 billion, American Express said.</p><p>Consumer sentiment did improve this month, rising by 11.4 points to 103.3, the first time the Conference Board Consumer Index surpassed 100 since January 2025. The increase signals optimism about the current business and labor market, likely pushed by the results of the midterm elections, which cleared some uncertainty, Conference Board economists suggested in their Tuesday report.</p><p>Koval is gearing up for the holidays with a slew of special releases, including its Thresh and Winnow Millet Whiskey. She said the last four months of the year can make or break a spirits business.</p><p>“We're relying a lot more on the holidays than we may have in the past,” Hart said.</p><div class="Enhancement" Ravenswood Ave.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The company is one of about 40 distilleries in Chicago and among 2,100 nationwide, a total that has declined by the hundreds over the last few years. In 2026, more U.S. distilleries are expected to close than open, a first since the American Craft Spirits Association started tracking the data in 2016. </p><p>Koval has been hit by a crosswind of consumer shifts encouraging less alcohol consumption, from the wellness movement and the growth of weight-loss drugs, like GLP-1s, to the popularity of recreational cannabis use and the lingering social effects of the pandemic, according to Hart, who also serves as a consultant to craft liquor businesses.</p><p>“People just don’t go out as much,” she said.</p><p>But the Ravenswood establishment is aiming to break the trend Saturday afternoon, when the distillery hosts the Ravenswood Makers Market.</p><p>“It should be a fun day,” Hart said.</p><p>Frontera, who also runs a public relations firm, expects her gift shop to see a modest rebound on Small Business Saturday, buoyed by promotional campaigns from the Lincoln Park Chamber of Commerce.</p><p>She said October was the top-selling month at Holly House’s Lincoln Park location, which sells Christmas ornaments, handmade accessories, mystery books and other items. But November has been a dud.</p><p>“I just really hope people don't lose that Christmas magic and help small businesses because I'm starting to feel a very bah humbug vibe,” Frontera said. “We just haven't seen people. They're not buying anything.”</p><h3></h3><p>Werk Force Brewing Co. has been battling tariffs on German malts and Canadian raw materials for over a year. The Plainfield brewer imports the majority of its canning aluminum from Canada, where it also sources bottles for its flagship Russian imperial stout, Sleepy Bear.</p><p>“It’s been a roller coaster,” owner Brandon Wright said. “We’re pivoting all the time, just trying to figure out and anticipate what changes can happen.”</p><p>He said Thanksgiving week is a big revenue generator — its flagship barrel-aged stout was released Wednesday, and variants are dropping other days of the week.</p><h3>More than a service</h3><p>In Niles, Kouklas Greek Eatery is booked for 300 guests Saturday, a strong turnout highlighting its early success. </p><p>The restaurant, which specializes in shareable contemporary takes on classic Greek dishes, opened on New Year’s Eve. It was one of two Illinois restaurants featured on The New York Times 50 Best Restaurants list this year. </p><p>“We've been, fortunately, extremely busy,” managing partner Audrey Witte said.</p><p>Guillotine opened in June on a bustling section of Chicago Avenue, home to art galleries, eateries and funky shops like <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/small-business/2025/05/19/beyonce-chicago-concerts-beyhive-alcalas-western-wear" target="_blank" >Alcala’s Western Wear</a>.</p><p>Bikard left an unfulfilling consulting job in Paris to start the pastry shop, which specializes in handmade traditional French offerings like kouign-amann, chouquettes and croissants.</p><p>The launch has gone well, despite some typical growing pains like adjusting staffing, inventory and raw materials to meet demand.</p><p>She said Small Business Saturday provides an opportunity to showcase independent businesses when big-box retailers typically grab the attention during the holiday season.</p><p>"Of course, it's always easier to buy something from Amazon or wherever," Bikard said. It showcased her mixed-media prints and sculptures often incorporating the work of her father, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2021/5/7/22423108/eugene-eda-wade-painter-wall-respect-black-arts-movement-public-malcolm-x-college-doors" >Eugene “Eda” Wade</a>, a famed muralist of Chicago’s Black Art movement from the mid-1960s to 1970s.</p><p>A few months later she was tapped to curate Local Soul, a year-old collective at Navy Pier showcasing apparel, food, art and other items from hometown creatives and designers. Wade wants to help scale Chicago brands while making art more accessible for visitors, hence the $10 postcards of prints from local artists and brand stickers that have become big sellers.</p><p>“The goal is to feature brands from all 77 neighborhoods of Chicago and beyond,” Wade said. “Given the state of the economy, we’re creating more opportunities to support them."</p><p>JJ Salazar, founder of Bangin Brows + Skin in Lincoln Park, said small businesses must often work harder than larger brands to attract customers. </p><p>“When you shop small, you're not just buying a service," she said. "You're backing a mom of three who built this business one brow at a time."</p>
